bodyBlocks.text: The investigation began with one alum’s report about one longtime faculty member and administrator.

According to the report, an Academy alum from the 1970s contacted Interlochen about a longtime faculty member and administrator. Interlochen and its board retained Sanghavi Law Office in September 2024 to investigate reports involving that individual, identified in the report only as Respondent 1.

In June 2025, the school expanded the assignment to include reports from any decade involving faculty, staff or other adults affiliated with the Academy. Investigators ultimately received information concerning the Camp as well. Interlochen later added targeted outreach to people it believed might have information concerning Jeffrey Epstein, a former camper and donor.

The law firm said it had no prior relationship with Interlochen. The institution helped locate participants and supplied available records, while the investigative team said it retained autonomy over the information it gathered and the observations it published. Interlochen asked the team to prioritize physical misconduct and complete a report during summer 2026.

Some work remained unfinished when the report was released. Investigators said they would continue speaking with additional people who came forward, and the report acknowledges that some interviews and follow-up outreach had not been completed. The published document is therefore a substantial historical record, but not a final census.
What investigators did, and what they deliberately did not do
Source note: S1, pp. 4–10; S2, methodology FAQ.

The investigative team conducted approximately 180 interviews with roughly 150 distinct people. Participants included alumni, relatives, current and former employees, people accused of misconduct and others with relevant knowledge. Some people provided written information instead of, or in addition to, an interview.

Investigators reviewed available student and personnel files, contacted respondents when possible and interviewed ten current or former employees about what the institution may have known and how it responded.
The historical record had obvious limits.

More than one-third of the 47 respondents were deceased. Only four respondents discussed in the main decade-by-decade section participated in interviews. None of the employees interviewed about institutional response had served as an administrator during the 1960s or 1970s. Some former employees did not respond, declined to participate or had died.

The documentary record was also incomplete. Investigators reviewed personnel files when they existed, but Interlochen said its current personnel-file retention period was seven years and that some older files had previously been purged. Some accused adults were donors, trustees, visitors or people for whom an employee file would not ordinarily exist. Other people could not be identified from the information participants remembered decades later.

For privacy, the report deliberately omits or generalizes some dates, disciplines, job titles, locations and biographical details. That decision protects alumni, but it also limits what an outside reader can independently reconstruct.

Most important, the firm did not attempt to adjudicate each account. Its report says the team did not determine whether the conduct occurred as reported. Interlochen’s accompanying public explanation states even more directly that investigators did not make individual credibility determinations and accepted information as true for purposes of compiling the report.

Those distinctions govern how the report should be described. A firsthand account is not a conviction. A personnel file documenting a contemporaneous complaint carries different weight from a later recollection. An admission is different from a denial. The absence of a surviving record does not prove that no report was made, and a reported disclosure does not by itself establish that senior leadership received or understood it.
The report contains all of those evidence types, sometimes within the same respondent entry.
What “approximately 70 accounts” actually counts
Source note: S1, pp. 7–8, 12–75; S2, respondent-identification FAQ. The arithmetic below is Boho News’ reconstruction from the report’s published section totals.

The figure repeated most often from the report is approximately 70 firsthand accounts of physical conduct of a sexual nature involving 47 respondents. The report does not say that those accounts came from 70 different people.

The report explains that when one person described conduct involving multiple adults, the conduct involving each adult was counted separately. It also separates physical conduct from a broader body of reports involving sexual comments, grooming, propositions, intrusive questions, boundary violations and other nonphysical behavior. Those additional concerns are not included in the headline total.

The published section totals allow the figure to be reconstructed. The main decade-organized section covers Respondents 2 through 46 and contains 61 separately counted firsthand accounts involving 45 respondents:

bodyBlocks.caption: Accounts and respondents by earliest reported decade

bodyBlocks.text: A separate section records seven accounts involving Respondent 1, whom Interlochen later identified as Byron Hanson. Another separate section records two accounts involving Epstein.
Together, the three sections total:

The report calls the total approximate and separately explains that post-Interlochen conduct may be included when it is relevant to conduct that began or occurred at Interlochen. Several respondent summaries include conduct after graduation. The report does not publish the number of unique alumni represented by the approximately 70 separately counted accounts.

The figure should not be converted into “70 victims,” “70 proven assaults” or necessarily “70 different alumni.” The report describes approximately 70 separately counted firsthand accounts involving 47 respondents.

bodyBlocks.text: How the report organizes seven decades of accounts
Source note: S1, pp. 11–75; S2.
The report says the conduct described to investigators began in the 1950s and continued into the 2010s, with most reports involving conduct before 2000.

The decade headings group each respondent by the earliest reported conduct involving that person. A respondent placed in the 1970s section stays there even when the report describes later conduct. The chart above therefore reflects the report’s organization, not the annual prevalence of misconduct. Several publicly identified respondents had long tenures at Interlochen.

Interlochen publicly identified Hanson, Respondent 1, as a faculty member and administrator from 1960 until 2015. It identified John “Jack” Hood, Respondent 8, as a faculty member and administrator from 1963 to 1979 who later returned in seasonal roles through 2004. It identified Charlie McWhorter, Respondent 19, as a trustee from 1970 to 1999.

Interlochen said it named those deceased respondents because investigators received multiple firsthand reports reflecting repeated and pervasive conduct and because public identification would not interfere with prosecution. The institution also publicly identified former faculty member Thomas Clower, saying he was convicted in 2005 after Interlochen reported the conduct and terminated him.

The remaining respondents are not publicly named in the report. Some are deceased; some are living. Interlochen says none currently works for the institution and that it supplied all respondent identities to the Grand Traverse County prosecutor and sheriff.
Those are institutional statements. The public materials reviewed by Boho News do not independently establish the present employment or volunteer activities of unnamed living respondents.
What the report describes
Source note: S1, pp. 4, 11–77.
The accounts cover a wide range of alleged conduct and boundary violations.

Some accounts describe sexual comments, intrusive questions, propositions, unwanted kissing or touching over clothing. Others describe adults escalating private lessons or mentoring relationships into sexual contact. Several participants described purported romantic relationships with faculty or staff, sometimes continuing for months or years. The report emphasizes that a student’s description of a relationship as consensual does not erase the adult’s professional responsibility or the power imbalance inherent in an educational setting.
The reported settings recur:

items: faculty offices and practice rooms;
private lessons;
faculty homes;
dormitories and residence-life rooms;
cars and school-related travel;
hotels and out-of-state trips;
cabins and unoccupied campus buildings;
wooded areas, camping trips and a nearby lake;
donor or trustee interactions;
trips that continued after a student left Interlochen.

bodyBlocks.text: Not every account describes the same severity. Not every respondent faced multiple reports. Some participants said they never told an adult at Interlochen. Some said friends or relatives knew. Some described contemporaneous reporting. Some institutional files contained warnings, complaints or disciplinary records. A few respondents participated and denied, partly acknowledged or described the conduct differently. Many could not be interviewed because they had died.

The accounts also vary in evidentiary support. Some rely on a participant’s later recollection; others are accompanied by contemporaneous disclosures, institutional files, respondent statements or criminal records.
What the report says Interlochen knew
Source note: S1, pp. 11–72. The six-part notice spectrum below is Boho News’ analytical framework for comparing differently supported entries.
There is no single answer across all 47 respondents.

In some cases, an alum said the conduct was never reported and investigators found no evidence that Interlochen knew. In others, participants believed adults must have seen warning signs but could not identify a direct report. Some people said they reported conduct, while no surviving record of that report could be found. Elsewhere, personnel files documented contemporaneous concerns, meetings, warnings, leaves, resignations, terminations, recommendations or referrals to authorities.
For comparison, the entries fall into six broad categories:

items: No contemporaneous report identified.
Possible informal awareness or visible warning signs.
A report described by a participant, but no surviving institutional record.
A contemporaneous complaint or concern documented in a file.
Institutional action documented.
Action accompanied by contradictory conduct, such as continued employment, rehiring or recommendations after notice.

bodyBlocks.text: Several entries pair alumni accounts with surviving institutional records.
Respondent 14: recommendations after meetings about sexual conduct
Source: S1, pp. 29–30. Investigator-recorded allegation plus personnel-file summary.

One alum described a faculty member repeatedly crossing sexual boundaries during private lessons in the 1970s. She told investigators that she eventually reported the conduct to Academy leadership, that other people came forward and that she was told the respondent would be asked to resign.

The personnel file reflected multiple meetings with Respondent 14 concerning sexual conduct toward an unidentified person. According to the report, an administrator wrote a recommendation letter within days of the third meeting. Interlochen then placed the respondent on leave. A second administrator wrote another recommendation approximately a month later, and the respondent was released from his contract at his own request roughly another month after that.

The public report does not disclose what the recommendation letters said, where they were sent or whether the recipients were told about the concerns. Those records remain central to determining what happened after Respondent 14 left Interlochen.
Respondent 31: contemporaneous reports, delayed termination and multiple recommendations
Source: S1, pp. 48–50. Investigator-recorded allegations, employee recollections and personnel-file summary.

Two alumni described sexual conduct by Respondent 31. One said she reported what had happened to a staff member and later met with senior administrators. She recalled feeling blamed and condescended to rather than supported.

The personnel file reflected contemporaneous reports involving that alum and another student. It also showed that Respondent 31 was terminated approximately four months after the report. After Interlochen knew of the conduct, according to the investigators, administrators and a teacher wrote multiple recommendation letters for him.
The existence of a recommendation does not establish that the writer concealed known misconduct. The letters, dates, recipients and surrounding correspondence are not included in the public report.
Respondent 32: warnings across years before resignation
Source: S1, pp. 50–52. Investigator-recorded allegations, respondent interview and personnel-file summary.

Two alumni described sexual conduct by Respondent 32. During his interview with investigators, the respondent denied intercourse with students but acknowledged sexual touching involving one alum and “probably” another student. He described a relationship that began while one alum was still a student and characterized its evolution in familial, friendly and romantic terms.

The personnel file reflected contemporaneous concerns in the 1980s and 1990s. In one instance, an administrator warned that unprofessional touching would result in termination. In the 2000s, one alum sent a letter describing conduct from the 1980s. Respondent 32 resigned approximately six weeks later, and an administrator told investigators the resignation was accepted in part because of the alum’s report.
This is one of the few entries that combines institutional records with a partial acknowledgment from the respondent.
Respondent 41: three documented nonphysical concerns, no discipline beyond recording them
Source: S1, pp. 62–63. Investigator-recorded allegation, counsel’s denial and personnel-file summary.
One alum described boundary-crossing physical conduct by a residence-life employee. Through counsel, Respondent 41 denied any improper conduct and declined an interview.

The personnel file did not show that Interlochen knew about the conduct described by that alum. It did show three separate contemporaneous reports of nonphysical sexual conduct involving students. Investigators wrote that no disciplinary action beyond documenting those concerns was taken.
The file did not corroborate the alum’s specific account. It did, however, document other concerns involving the same adult.
Respondent 46: a recommendation against rehiring, continued access and later reporting to authorities
Source: S1, pp. 71–72. Investigator-recorded allegation and personnel-file summary. The report states the respondent did not answer outreach.
An alum described sexual contact by a residence-life employee after the adult supplied him alcohol and the student became severely impaired. The alum said he did not report the encounter at the time.

The personnel file, however, contained earlier and later warning signs. A camp supervisor had recommended that Respondent 46 not be rehired because displays of affection toward campers made counselors uncomfortable. An administrator hired him anyway, attributing the problem to a difficult supervisory relationship.

During a later academic year, administrators questioned the respondent about whether anything inappropriate or physical had happened involving a student. Another administrator raised concerns that Respondent 46 took individual students off campus and had students alone in his room. A temporary hold on his next contract was lifted, and he continued working.

After another student and parent reported conduct, Interlochen notified child protective services within approximately two days, cooperated with a detective, began its own investigation, barred the respondent from campus and instructed him to stop contacting students.

The same personnel history records an earlier warning that did not prevent rehiring, later concerns that did not immediately end access, and an eventual report to child protection and law enforcement.
A pattern of uneven response
Source note: S1, pp. 11–72, especially pp. 29–30, 48–52, 62–63, 66–68 and 71–72. Interpretive conclusions are labeled as Boho News analysis.

The report does not show a uniform institutional response. In some cases no contemporaneous report was identified; in others administrators acted promptly. In the entry for Respondent 43, the report says Interlochen placed the employee on leave, contacted law enforcement, preserved and searched electronic records, terminated the employee after an arrest, and that the employee later pleaded guilty to attempted fourth-degree criminal sexual conduct. (S1, pp. 66–68.)

It also documents cases involving recommendations after notice, warnings without immediate separation, concerns recorded without discipline, unexplained departures and conflicting recollections about whether a person resigned or was terminated.

The surviving record is uneven. Some files describe recommendations after notice, warnings without immediate separation, rehiring despite prior concerns and decisions that left access in place. Other entries describe reporting to law enforcement, leave, termination and later criminal convictions.

Without the underlying recommendation letters, separation records and related correspondence, the report does not establish what outside institutions were told. Those records are a priority for further reporting.
The conditions that recur across decades
Source note: S1, pp. 81–88. The investigators identified themes but did not make causal findings.

After the respondent summaries, investigators identified six themes that participants said shaped the environment in which misconduct occurred: limited communication with family; student vulnerability; adult-student power imbalances; adults’ access to students; gaps in oversight and a permissive environment; and barriers to reporting.

The report does not claim those conditions caused every reported event, and alumni described many of the same features as strengths of an Interlochen education. Close relationships with teachers could provide exceptional mentorship while also blurring professional boundaries. Sponsor groups could give children far from home a substitute family while bringing students into private homes. One-on-one artistic instruction could be educationally valuable while placing students alone with powerful adults.

bodyBlocks.text: Isolation from home

Before mobile phones, email and routine internet access, boarding students had limited ways to tell family members what was happening day to day. Participants described one-way hall phones, limited mail access and a remote campus that parents could not easily reach.
Distance did not cause abuse, but it reduced the number of adults outside the institution who could notice a change or receive a disclosure quickly.
Children treated as unusually mature
Several alumni described arriving young, inexperienced and unprepared to recognize grooming or sexual boundary violations. Others said Interlochen treated students as unusually independent or adult.

Treating students as unusually mature could shift responsibility away from adults. Artistic ability, independence and life away from home did not change the professional duties of teachers, counselors, trustees or donors.
Prestige, scholarships and artistic futures
Faculty members could control lessons, casting, recommendations, scholarships and professional introductions. Participants described adults invoking their connections or making students feel chosen.

At an arts institution, that authority could extend beyond grades. A student could reasonably believe one teacher controlled auditions, recommendations, scholarships or access to a professional career.

The report also describes private instruction as a routine feature of arts education. Some rooms historically lacked windows, or their windows were covered. Physical touch can legitimately be part of teaching breathing, posture or technique. Those facts made it harder for students to distinguish appropriate instruction from boundary crossing and gave adults plausible access to students’ bodies in private settings.
Homes, sponsor groups and residence life

Interlochen used sponsor groups to create a sense of family for students living away from home. Alumni described dinners, movies, music and other gatherings at employees’ houses. Many remembered those experiences positively.
Others said group contact could become one-on-one contact, and that some adults used private homes to groom or engage in sexual conduct with students.

Residence-life staff occupied another position of unusual access. They lived near students and, according to some participants, sometimes acted more like peers or friends than supervisors. The report describes students being invited into staff rooms and boundary problems developing in the same spaces meant to provide care and oversight.
Cars, trips, hotels and other private spaces
Participants described conduct during school trips, personal trips, car rides, hotel stays, camping trips, boat rides and visits to adults’ homes.
Institutionally authorized contact could therefore move from campus into private spaces with little oversight.
Donors and trustees

The report also describes broad historical access for adults who were not employees. Alumni said donors and trustees could visit classes and rehearsals, walk through student areas, obtain information about children and transport students off campus.
Several participants viewed Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s access as one example of that broader structure, rather than an isolated anomaly.
The donor-access issue extends beyond Epstein. Participants described ordinary practices that allowed wealthy supporters and trustees to obtain direct access to students.
A permissive environment and weak reporting routes
Some alumni described sexual relationships between adults and students as rumored, visible or tolerated. Others said they saw none of this. The report includes both experiences.

Participants described inconsistent sign-out rules, students staying overnight away from campus, adults drinking with students and employees failing to intervene when boundaries were visible. Some former students said they did not know where to report, believed they would not be believed or feared being punished, expelled or sent home.

Others worried about destroying a beloved teacher’s career or becoming known as the student responsible for an adult’s dismissal. Some had formed emotional attachments to the adults involved and did not understand the conduct as abuse until years later.
Other alumni said Interlochen responded promptly and made them feel believed. Those accounts provide a contrast to the cases involving delay, blame or no surviving record of a response.
Epstein’s place in the report
Source note: S1, pp. 73–75; S3; attached federal records E0014, E0020, E0023, E0024 and E0026.
Jeffrey Epstein takes up only a few pages of the report, but those pages connect the broader questions of donor access, scholarships, travel and contact with students.
Investigators contacted eight alumni whom Interlochen believed might have relevant information; six participated. Two described physical conduct of a sexual nature by Epstein.

One alum described meeting Epstein through Interlochen, tuition support, contact at the lodge once named for him, paid trips to New York while she was a student and repeated unwanted touching. A second alum described meeting Epstein through another Interlochen student, a paid New York trip after graduation and a sexual encounter involving a massage. The report says portions of the second account were corroborated. Her mother told investigators that she called Interlochen to warn that Epstein was preying on students, but investigators found no institutional record of that call.

The investigators expressly excluded public court filings and media reports from their Epstein section. The two-page summary is therefore not a complete public record of his relationship with Interlochen.

Boho News separately reviewed federal court records contained in the uploaded Epstein and Maxwell archive. A February 2020 grand-jury subpoena demanded Interlochen’s records of Epstein and Maxwell donations, tuition payments, other financial contributions and campus visits. A 1994 Interlochen letter thanked Epstein for a $200,000 lodge gift and described annual personal-use rights. Trial testimony from an Interlochen finance official authenticated donor correspondence and described the institution’s donor and student-record practices. Pilot testimony described repeated flights to Traverse City and visits to Interlochen. (E0014; E0020; E0024, document pp. 242–252; E0026, document pp. 123–124.)

bodyBlocks.text: A later installment will examine those records in full. For this overview, they establish that Epstein’s documented relationship with Interlochen extended beyond the two accounts summarized in the Sanghavi report. The subpoena and correspondence do not establish that Interlochen knew he was engaging in misconduct.

bodyBlocks.text: What participants said the conduct cost them
Source note: S1, pp. 77–81.
The report devotes a separate section to the effects participants attributed to the conduct.

Some said it changed how they remembered Interlochen, turning a place they had loved into one associated with betrayal or danger. Some described disruptions to their education, including changing teachers, abandoning an artistic discipline or losing confidence in their work. Others described effects on professional choices, mental health, trust, intimacy and later relationships.
The reported effects differed from person to person.

A person could value friendships, training and artistic opportunities while also describing serious harm. Some alumni maintained deep affection for Interlochen. Others avoided reunions, stopped donating or distanced themselves from the institution. Some said the conduct shaped their lives for decades; others described narrower effects.

Several alumni described both valuable training and lasting harm. Affection for the school did not negate what they said happened there, and the reported harm did not erase every positive part of their education.
What Interlochen says has changed
Source note: S1, pp. 89–95; S2. These are institutional policy descriptions and announced actions, not independent findings of effectiveness.
Interlochen released the report with an apology and a list of current safeguards and planned actions.

The institution says none of the 47 respondents currently works there. It says all respondent names were provided to the Grand Traverse County prosecutor and sheriff. It established a counseling support fund, announced a review of naming recognitions and committed to an arts installation honoring survivors.

The report’s current-practices section is based on policies and information supplied by Interlochen. It describes background checks, annual training, professional-boundary rules, mandated reporting, multiple reporting channels, restrictions on closed-door one-on-one contact, supervision requirements, visitor identification, security cameras and rules for off-campus and donor interactions.

The investigation did not independently test whether those policies are consistently understood, enforced or effective. A later article in this series will examine their implementation through records and interviews with the current Interlochen community.

The same principle applies to law-enforcement referrals. Interlochen says it supplied respondent identities to local authorities. The public materials reviewed for this article do not disclose the exact transmittal dates, case numbers, contents of the referrals or status of any resulting review.
What the report does not answer
Source note: S1, pp. 4–10, 73–75 and 89–95; S2; S3; Boho News analysis.
The report is the most extensive public account Boho News has reviewed concerning historical misconduct at Interlochen. Major questions remain:

items: How many unique alumni are represented by the approximately 70 separately counted accounts?
Which reported events, if any, could be independently substantiated beyond the evidence summarized in the report?
Were historical institutional responses adequate, and who made the relevant decisions?
What was contained in personnel, student or administrative files that no longer exist?
Do any living respondents currently work or volunteer around minors?
Why were some adults recommended, rehired or allowed continued access after concerns were documented?
What did outside institutions receive or learn when former Interlochen personnel applied elsewhere?
What did Interlochen’s 2009 and 2019 Epstein reviews examine, and what work product survives?
Was the reported warning call about Epstein made, and if so, who received it?
How many alumni never came forward, declined contact or could not be located?
Are the school’s current safeguards working as described?

bodyBlocks.text: The report also does not answer a question that will guide later reporting: whether Interlochen’s history and permissive access practices were publicly visible before Epstein began donating in 1990, and whether he or other outsiders deliberately exploited them. That remains an investigative hypothesis, not a finding of the report.
What the report establishes
Source note: S1; Boho News analysis.
For the first time, Interlochen has published a single document acknowledging that reports of sexual misconduct spanned generations, institutional roles and locations across the school and camp.

The report does not adjudicate the individual accounts, and publication is not the same as completed accountability. Its value lies in the record it assembles: firsthand accounts, contemporaneous disclosures, personnel-file summaries, respondent statements, institutional actions and gaps where the paper trail ends.

That record is now the starting point for further reporting. Boho News will use it to examine the school’s history before Epstein, the donor relationship documented in federal records, the fate of living respondents, the institution’s present safeguards and the public response to the report.
How Boho News reviewed the report
Boho News read the complete 97-page report and mapped each consequential claim to the report’s printed page numbers. This article distinguishes:

items: adjudicated facts and guilty pleas;
statements made by Interlochen;
allegations recorded from firsthand participants;
facts investigators said appeared in personnel or student files;
respondent admissions, denials and nonresponses;
federal court records;
Boho News analysis and unresolved questions.

bodyBlocks.text: Boho News preserved the report’s anonymization. We did not attempt to identify unnamed alumni or respondents through biographical clues, and descriptions of alleged conduct are limited to the detail needed to explain the record.

Interlochen’s public response, announced actions and policy descriptions are attributed throughout. For anonymous respondents used as examples, the article preserves the response recorded in the report: participation and partial acknowledgment, denial through counsel, death or nonresponse. It adds no identifying information.

A 14-week emergency medical technician course at Iowa Central Community College is the first program in the country approved to use a new federal version of the Pell Grant for short workforce credentials.

The U.S. Department of Education announced the approval Monday at the college’s Fort Dodge campus. Eligible students can now apply federal need-based aid to the EMT course, rather than having to choose only from longer certificate or degree programs that already fit traditional Pell rules.

The approval is narrow: it applies to one program, not every short course at Iowa Central or every workforce class in Iowa. Students still have to complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, qualify on financial need and enroll in a program the department has approved.

Workforce Pell expands the federal grant to accredited programs lasting at least eight weeks and no more than 15 weeks. Iowa Central’s EMT course sits near the upper end of that range and has operated long enough to meet the program’s one-year history requirement.

Congress and the Education Department attached performance conditions to that expansion. Programs must clear benchmarks for completion, job placement and graduate earnings, and they need approval from both a state governor and the federal education secretary.

Those requirements are meant to distinguish short programs that lead to work from classes that are merely brief. They do not show, on their own, that every approved program will deliver the same result for every student. The new federal system has not existed long enough to produce a public multi-year record under its own rules.

The final federal rule was published May 18 and took effect July 1. Iowa had opened its state application process in May, asking colleges and training providers to submit programs in high-demand fields for the governor’s review before federal submission.

For a qualifying student, the immediate change is financing. Pell Grants generally do not have to be repaid, but an award is not automatic and the exact amount depends on the student’s federal-aid calculation and enrollment circumstances.

The approval therefore removes one barrier without erasing the rest of the cost equation. Students may still face transportation, supplies, testing, scheduling and living expenses while completing an intensive 14-week course.

The subject of the first approval is significant. EMT training leads to a licensed emergency-response role that communities depend on, and the short format is designed to move students into the workforce quickly. The federal announcement did not publish a new forecast of Iowa EMT vacancies or promise that every graduate would be hired.

Iowa’s application process requires providers to document labor demand, program history and student outcomes. Federal review adds the Workforce Pell thresholds. Together, the steps create a chain of accountability from the college to the state and then to Washington.

What comes next is measurable: how many eligible students use the grant, whether they complete the course, whether they obtain jobs and whether earnings remain high enough for the program to keep qualifying. Those results will matter more than the ceremonial first.

Other states and colleges can follow the same route, but the Education Department’s announcement did not provide a complete list or timetable for pending applications. Iowa Central is first, not necessarily alone for long.

June brought 374 preliminary tornado reports across the United States while drought still covered 47.8% of the contiguous country at month’s end, a split-screen climate picture of intense Midwest storms and persistent dryness across much of the interior West.

NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information said Illinois recorded 91 preliminary tornado reports, Indiana 69 and Missouri 32. Each total set a new June record for that state, according to the agency’s July 9 national climate assessment.

The word “preliminary” matters. Storm reports are reviewed and can be consolidated or reclassified, so 374 is not the final confirmed tornado count for June.

The contiguous United States received 3.23 inches of precipitation in June, 0.31 inch above the 20th-century average. That ranked in the wettest third of the 132-year record.

Yet the national mean masks sharp regional differences. The West and Southwest remained below 70% of their average year-to-date precipitation, even as rain eased drought across parts of the Plains, Midwest, lower Mississippi and Ohio valleys, Southeast and far Northeast.

The June 30 U.S. Drought Monitor placed about 47.8% of the contiguous country in drought. NOAA described that as a decrease of about 10.5% since the start of June, but drought persisted or intensified across much of the Northwest, Southwest, Great Basin and Rockies.

The contiguous U.S. average temperature was 70.6 degrees Fahrenheit, 2.2 degrees above the 20th-century average. That put June in the warmest third of the historical record rather than at the top of it.

Above- to much-above-average temperatures covered much of the West, Southwest, southern Plains, Florida, Mid-Atlantic and Northeast. Parts of the northern Rockies and Plains ran below average, while portions of the Midwest and Southeast were closer to average.

Across the first half of 2026, the West and Southwest climate regions posted their warmest January-through-June periods on record. That longer interval is a separate result from the national June ranking and should not be collapsed into a claim that every region had its warmest June.

Hawaiʻi averaged 7.03 inches of precipitation in June, nearly twice its 1991–2020 average of 3.60 inches and the state’s second-wettest June in the record used by NOAA.

Its January-through-June total reached 54.62 inches, 24.87 inches above average and the highest first-half total in the state record, which begins in 1991.

The June assessment does not describe one uniform national condition. A wetter-than-average contiguous U.S. total can coexist with record-warm and dry conditions in the West because regional deficits and surpluses are combined into one number.

The same caution applies to the tornado total. A high concentration in three Midwest states drove the month’s severe-weather headline, while drought and heat remained the more important signals across large western areas.

NOAA’s monthly assessment is a snapshot based on the data available when published. Final tornado counts, later climate-quality control and subsequent drought maps can refine individual values without changing the core June contrast.

Twenty-one fossil footprints on an ancient lakeshore in northern Kenya record eight hominins moving across the same surface about 1.43 million years ago, giving researchers an unusually direct look at body size and possible group movement in Paranthropus boisei.

The GaJi10 trackway, described July 27 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, also carries deeper prints from hippopotamuses, antelope and other animals. Volcanic ash in the surrounding Koobi Fora Formation provided the age estimate.

Researchers attribute the hominin tracks to Paranthropus based on foot anatomy and movement patterns developed in earlier comparative work. The assignment is an interpretation, not a genetic identification: the footprints are unexpectedly large and overlap in size with tracks linked to Homo erectus, which lived in the same region.

Smithsonian geologist Kay Behrensmeyer first noticed a deep hippopotamus print in 1978 while a field crew exposed the sediment layer. Brushing the surface revealed two hominin tracks. After initial study, the team reburied the site in sand to protect it.

Researchers returned in 2016 and 2023 and uncovered a much broader track surface. The final mapped assemblage contains 21 hominin prints associated with eight individuals, plus numerous animal tracks.

Footprints preserve behavior on a time scale that bones rarely can: a step is made in seconds, and several prints on one surface can show which individuals were present together. They do not reveal how long a group remained together or the relationships among its members.

Measurements of the prints produced maximum body-size estimates near 1.8 meters, or 6 feet, and 75 kilograms, or 165 pounds. Those values are larger than many estimates built from the limited Paranthropus skeletal record and bring the largest track makers into the range often associated with Homo erectus.

That size overlap is scientifically important because both hominins occupied the Lake Turkana landscape. The authors favor Paranthropus for GaJi10 because of the shape and apparent gait of the tracks, while the body-size result expands rather than erases the uncertainty around species assignment.

Most of the prints are adult-sized and run in broadly similar directions. The team interprets the surface as evidence that multiple individuals, possibly mostly adult males, traveled together.

That pattern may point to a more complex social structure than isolated bones imply. But one preserved moment cannot establish whether the group was stable, how mating worked, or why the individuals crossed the mudflat.

The eastern Lake Turkana region now contains hundreds of hominin footprints deposited over more than 100,000 years. Combined with earlier sites preserving both Paranthropus-like and Homo erectus-like tracks, the record shows that multiple human relatives repeatedly used the same lakeshore environments.

The team plans more fieldwork in Kenya. Each new surface can test whether the GaJi10 pattern was exceptional or part of a recurring way these hominins moved through the landscape.

Owners of nearly 463,000 Kia Tellurides are being told to park outside and away from buildings until dealers complete a second repair for a front-seat motor that can overheat and catch fire.

National Highway Traffic Safety Administration campaign 26V430 covers 462,869 vehicles from model years 2020 through 2024. The same vehicles were recalled in 2024 under campaign 24V407, but Kia’s defect chronology says investigators later found both sporadic repair-workmanship problems and another way the seat switch could be damaged.

Kia plans to begin notifying owners Aug. 13. Until the new remedy is completed, NHTSA says affected vehicles should be parked outdoors, away from structures and other vehicles, whether or not the first recall repair was performed.

The problem sits in the front power-seat controls. If the slide cover or knob is hit, the switch can become dislodged, internally misaligned or damaged. That can command the seat motor to run continuously, generating enough heat to melt components or start a fire while the SUV is parked or moving.

Under the 2024 campaign, dealers were instructed to reinforce the switch or replace it when necessary. Kia later inspected repaired vehicles and found sporadic workmanship issues, including cases where a switch may have been reinforced when replacement was required.

The company also investigated whether a person entering the vehicle could strike the seat slide knob with enough twisting force to misalign the switch even when the back cover remained in place.

Kia’s filing says its safety office identified 18 unique incidents received from October 2024 through April 2026: seven localized seat or under-seat fires and 11 cases of localized seat-motor melting. The chronology reports no injuries, crashes or fatalities.

Those counts describe reports known to the company during its investigation; they are not an estimate of the probability that any one vehicle will catch fire. The safety action is broad because an overheating motor can ignite while the vehicle is unattended.

Dealers will install an electronic fuse assembly designed to interrupt power if the seat motor operates continuously. The repair is free under the safety-recall process.

Owners can search NHTSA.gov by the vehicle identification number or license plate and should look specifically for campaign 26V430. A vehicle previously marked complete under 24V407 may still need the new remedy.

NHTSA’s Vehicle Safety Hotline is 888-327-4236. Kia customer service is 800-333-4542. Owners who smell burning, see smoke or observe heat damage should stop using the vehicle and contact emergency services if there is an active fire.

Four labor unions and an employee benefit plan agreed to pay $3.85 million to settle federal civil claims that they improperly obtained Paycheck Protection Program loans, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York announced.

The agreement covers the International Union of Journeymen and Allied Trades, United Service Workers Union, Home Healthcare Workers of America, Service Professionals Union Local 726 and the United Welfare Fund's welfare division.

According to the Justice Department, the five entities received a combined $3,316,966 in PPP loans after submitting applications between April 16 and April 20, 2020. Each later applied for and received full forgiveness.

The entities were organized under section 501(c)(5) of the tax code. The government said organizations in that category were not eligible for PPP loans under the rules in effect when the applications were submitted.

The settlement resolves allegations under the False Claims Act. It is a civil resolution, not a criminal conviction, and some of the Justice Department's account describes allegations contained in the complaint.

As part of the agreement, however, the defendants admitted specified conduct. The Justice Department said each entity acknowledged certifying that it was eligible and acknowledged that, before applying, its bank contact had been advised by a Small Business Administration regional employee that only organizations under sections 501(c)(3) and 501(c)(19) were eligible.

The government joined a private whistleblower lawsuit that had initially been filed under seal. The False Claims Act permits private parties to bring certain cases on the government's behalf and allows the United States to intervene.

The settlement amount is larger than the original loan total, reflecting the resolution negotiated under the civil enforcement process. The public release does not provide a defendant-by-defendant allocation of the $3.85 million payment.

The case was handled by the U.S. Attorney's Office's Civil Frauds Unit. The settlement closes the claims covered by the agreement while preserving a public record of the admissions and the government's enforcement position.

The Library of Congress will open its August Thursday-evening programming with K-pop activities, a trivia event and an outdoor screening of the 1995 film “Apollo 13,” according to the institution's event schedule.

Two K-pop programs are planned for Aug. 6. From 5 to 8 p.m., visitors can hear a curated playlist, decorate a custom light stick and view materials from the Asian Division, Music Division and American Folklife Center.

A separate K-pop trivia program begins at 6 p.m. in room LJ-119. The Library said participants will be able to form teams, examine a special collections display and speak with staff members familiar with its Korean cultural holdings.

At 8 p.m., the Summer Movies on the Lawn series is scheduled to show “Apollo 13” on the North Lawn. The Library said no ticket is required for the outdoor screening, while the indoor evening programs use free registration.

The month's music schedule continues Aug. 13 with Amanda Pascali in the Coolidge Auditorium. The American Folklife Center artist is expected to perform music drawing on folk, Americana, Mediterranean, Balkan and Latin influences as part of the center's 50th anniversary.

On Aug. 27, banjo player Tray Wellington and his band are scheduled for a 6 p.m. Café Concert in the Great Hall, combining bluegrass, jazz, folk and contemporary roots music.

Live! at the Library also extends access to the Thomas Jefferson Building and exhibitions from 5 to 8 p.m. on Thursdays. Visitors may enter the Main Reading Room and view “The Declaration's Promise” exhibition during the evening hours.

The exhibition includes historical materials such as Thomas Jefferson's rough draft of the Declaration of Independence and Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, alongside cultural objects and multimedia displays.

Event registration, capacity and weather conditions may affect individual programs. The Library's official event listings remain the controlling source for last-minute changes.

The film lasts only about 45 seconds: a magician winds up a human-shaped automaton, the figure grows, strikes back and is hammered down to doll size. For more than a century, viewers knew Georges Méliès’s “Gugusse and the Automaton” largely by reputation.

Now the 1897 trick short is streaming again after Library of Congress technicians identified a surviving print among roughly 10 battered nitrate reels and spent more than a week repairing, scanning and stabilizing it.

The recovery appears in the Library’s July–August magazine and National Screening Room catalog. The catalog lists the French Star Film production as probably photographed in 1897 and notes that the surviving digital copy ends abruptly but appears complete.

When the reels reached the National Audio-Visual Conservation Center in Culpeper, Virginia, some cans were rusted, some film had crumbled and other strips had fused together. Staff examined the material frame by frame rather than risk running it through a projector.

A black star on an automaton’s pedestal helped reveal what they had. The action matched a film listed as Star Film catalog number 111: Méliès, playing the magician Gugusse, confronts a Pierrot figure that begins as a mechanical doll and becomes an unruly human-sized opponent.

The Library describes it as the first screen appearance of what might be called a robot. That wording matters. The film predates the word “robot” by more than two decades, and its character draws on the older stage tradition of clockwork automatons.

The reels came from the family of William DeLyle Frisbee, a western Pennsylvania farmer and teacher who also traveled with early motion pictures. His great-grandson Bill McFarland eventually drove the inherited cache from Grand Rapids, Michigan, to the Library in September 2025.

The films had passed through basements, barns, garages and a small trunk. That chain was far from archival, but it kept material that could not safely be projected from being discarded. The cache also held another Méliès film from 1900 and fragments of an early Thomas Edison title.

The recovered “Gugusse” print is not the camera negative. The Library says it is a duplicate at least three generations removed from the original, evidence of the copying and circulation that helped some early films survive after their masters vanished.

Technicians repaired the fragile nitrate stock, scanned it and stabilized the digital image. The work took more than a week. It did not erase every scratch, flicker or missing edge; those marks document the physical history of the surviving copy.

Méliès made more than 500 films, but most original negatives disappeared. Some were melted for their silver and celluloid during World War I, and the filmmaker later burned more. About 300 titles are known to survive, according to the Library, which holds roughly 60.

The recovered short expands that record by less than a minute, yet its subject bridges two histories: Méliès’s experiments with cinematic illusion and the long cultural idea of artificial figures escaping human control.

Its new availability is also the final preservation step that matters to the public. The catalog entry includes a downloadable viewing copy and a rights note saying the Library knows of no U.S. copyright restriction on the vast majority of films in the collection. A work once accessible only as a title in film history can again be watched as a moving image.

articles.body:
The Library of Congress has turned 4,000 square feet on the ground floor of its Thomas Jefferson Building into a research room designed for a group that rarely gets its own federal reading space: children and teenagers.

The Source: Where Curiosity Sparks Discovery opened May 9 and is designed especially for visitors ages 8 to 15, along with families and school groups. A new July/August Library of Congress Magazine feature shows the finished gallery and explains how its interactive stations are meant to make research feel like an active hunt rather than a formal assignment.

The room's most recognizable object is an animated card catalog. Opening its drawers can trigger collection-based scenes, including the tornado from The Wizard of Oz, a rocket launch and Rosa Parks' pancake recipe. The device uses the shape of an old research tool to introduce material held in many formats.

Elsewhere, seven Library staff members appear in short videos at a research desk, describing their work and suggesting items to explore. A large digital Source Book lets visitors assemble and share a collage from collection images, making their own trail through what they found.

The Library says the room contains hundreds of digitized and replica items spanning image, film, sound and text collections. The use of reproductions is important: young visitors can manipulate and compare material without putting fragile originals at risk.

The Source also treats research as a conversation. Staff and volunteers run scheduled Source Spotlight demonstrations, and a free Source Guide gives families a structure for a self-directed visit. The Library recommends allowing 30 to 45 minutes, though the gallery is built to support different paths rather than one fixed sequence.

The design was not produced only for young people; children helped shape it. The Library convened a youth advisory council of about two dozen children ages 8 to 12 in fall 2021. They reacted to early designs, tested ideas and offered blunt feedback about what felt inviting.

Weston Moats, one of those advisers, is pictured in the magazine feature inside the completed gallery. The visible result is a room with saturated orange fixtures, large-scale media and many points of entry—an environment that presents federal collections without mimicking an adult reading room.

The gallery is free, but visiting rules still apply. Children under 16 must remain with an adult. During Washington's summer and other school breaks, public hours are Tuesday through Friday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. During the school year, weekday public hours begin at 1 p.m.; Saturday hours remain 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

School and organized groups can use workshop programs or request free timed-entry tickets for visits during public hours. The Source is immediately to the right of the Jefferson Building's main entrance on the ground floor.

The new room does not make every part of Library research child-accessible, and its displays rely on selected digitized or replica objects rather than open access to the full physical collection. Its more consequential experiment is narrower: whether a national library can teach primary-source habits—asking questions, comparing formats and tracing evidence—before visitors think of research as something reserved for specialists.

Louisville Ladder is recalling about 1.77 million attic stairway ladders in the United States because spreader bolts can break and cause a user to fall, the Consumer Product Safety Commission announced Thursday.

The company has received 11 reports of bolts breaking, including one injury report involving the neck, head and back. About 13,054 additional units were sold in Canada.

The recall covers specified Louisville, Featherlite, Lite and Century brand attic stairway ladders equipped with gas struts. It does not mean every ladder sold under those brands is affected.

Owners should stop using a covered ladder immediately and check the model number printed on the inside of the attic door. CPSC directs consumers to the recall registration site, Atticstairwayrecall.expertinquiry.com, with that number available.

Louisville Ladder will provide a free repair kit containing two replacement quarter-inch spreader bolts, washers, lock nuts and installation instructions. Consumers should not resume use until the specified repair is installed.

The affected products were sold at The Home Depot, Lowe’s, Do It Best, Orgill and other retailers nationwide, and online at Amazon, from November 2012 through July 2026. Prices ranged from $170 to $600.

The product type matters because an attic stairway combines a folding ladder with hardware that supports opening, closing and weight-bearing. A failed spreader bolt can change the ladder’s geometry or support while someone is climbing.

The count of 11 reports does not establish a failure rate for the entire population. Consumer incident reports can be incomplete, and a large recall can be ordered when a component defect creates a meaningful fall hazard even if relatively few failures have been reported.

Consumers should rely on the model lookup rather than appearance alone. The official recall notice contains the affected model list, identification photographs and company contact information.

CPSC identifies the action as recall number 26-661. Anyone with an affected unit should keep it out of service, request the no-cost parts and follow the manufacturer’s installation instructions before using the ladder again.

articles.body:
Unemployment rates moved in opposite directions across nearly equal numbers of U.S. metropolitan areas in June, while statistically significant payroll growth remained concentrated in a small group of local economies, federal data released Wednesday show.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that jobless rates were higher than a year earlier in 184 of 387 metropolitan areas, lower in 178 and unchanged in 25. The national unemployment rate was 4.4 percent on a not-seasonally-adjusted basis, the same as in June 2025.

The payroll figures were considerably less balanced. Nonfarm employment increased significantly over the year in 15 metropolitan areas and decreased in three, while BLS classified the remaining 369 as essentially unchanged. BLS cites metro payroll changes in its release only when they are statistically significant at the 90 percent confidence level.

Dallas-Fort Worth-Arlington recorded the largest numerical payroll gain, adding 54,600 jobs from June 2025. Las Vegas-Henderson-North Las Vegas added 33,500, while Phoenix-Mesa-Chandler added 33,200. Athens-Clarke County, Georgia, posted the largest percentage increase at 4.1 percent.

The largest loss was in Washington-Arlington-Alexandria, where payroll employment fell by 83,500, or 2.4 percent. Portland-Vancouver-Hillsboro lost 25,700 jobs, or 2.1 percent, and Bloomington, Indiana, lost 3,300, or 4.2 percent.

Sioux Falls, South Dakota-Minnesota, had the lowest metro unemployment rate at 1.9 percent, followed by Rapid City, South Dakota, at 2.0 percent. El Centro, California, had the highest rate at 17.6 percent.

Lake Havasu City-Kingman, Arizona, recorded the largest year-over-year increase in its unemployment rate, rising 1.7 percentage points. Kokomo, Indiana, posted the largest decline, falling 1.9 percentage points.

The unemployment and payroll figures come from different BLS programs and measure different things. Unemployment estimates describe people by where they live, while payroll estimates count jobs by where establishments are located. Both sets of metro figures in the release are not seasonally adjusted.

The latest estimates remain subject to revision. BLS said it plans to publish preliminary benchmark revisions for March 2026 on Aug. 28, using employment counts derived from unemployment-insurance tax records. Final benchmark revisions for state and metropolitan series are scheduled with the January 2027 data release.

articles.body:
NASA-funded researchers will chase the August 12 total solar eclipse with a high-altitude jet and launch 86 scientific balloons from Iceland and Spain, turning the Moon’s shadow into a coordinated solar and atmospheric experiment.

The eclipse crosses Greenland, Iceland and Spain. A NASA WB-57 will fly along the path at about 460 miles per hour and 50,000 feet, above most clouds and much of the atmosphere that absorbs infrared light before it reaches ground telescopes.

Four cameras in the aircraft’s nose will record at least 20 images per second in multiple visible and infrared wavelengths. Scientists plan to examine fast-changing structures in the solar corona, suspended prominences and the relationship between coronal material and the solar wind.

Chasing the shadow extends the observation window. NASA says the longest view of the corona from the ground will be two minutes and 18 seconds, while the aircraft should remain in totality for nearly three minutes. That extra time produces more frames of a phenomenon that cannot be paused or repeated.

The instrument, called the SCIFLI Multispectral Airborne Imager, also flew during the April 2024 eclipse. The team adjusted exposure plans after bright features were overexposed in some earlier imagery and will use newer processing software to analyze the 2026 data sooner.

The balloon campaign targets a different layer of the event. In Iceland, two university teams plan to launch 80 balloons beginning 18 hours before totality and continuing until eight hours afterward, measuring how sudden darkness changes the atmospheric boundary layer near Earth’s surface.

Earlier eclipse campaigns found that the boundary layer thinned under clear skies but not cloudy ones. Iceland’s long August daylight creates a distinct test because its brief night may produce a weaker ordinary nighttime transition than researchers observed in 2023 and 2024.

In Spain, three teams plan six balloons with 360-degree cameras and ozone instruments. Ozone requires sunlight to form, and similar instruments measured a decline during the 2024 eclipse; the later time of day and different season give researchers another set of conditions to compare.

The flight and balloon counts are plans, not completed observations. Weather, launch conditions and aircraft operations can change them, and the scientific claims will come only after calibration and analysis. The experiment’s immediate news is its design: one brief shadow sampled across altitude, wavelength, geography and time.

articles.body:
NASA plans to send two identical small spacecraft toward the Moon in 2027 to test autonomous navigation, close-proximity operations and communications that future lunar missions may need without constant direction from Earth.

The mission, called CAPSTONE 02, is a paired-spacecraft successor in name and software lineage to the original Cislunar Autonomous Positioning System Technology Operations and Navigation Experiment.

NASA selected Colorado-based Advanced Space to develop and operate the demonstration. The agency described the launch year as a target, meaning schedule, integration and launch-provider milestones still stand between the announcement and flight.

Once in cislunar space, the spacecraft are designed to rendezvous and operate near one another. Relative navigation—knowing where one vehicle is with respect to the other—can support formation flying, inspection, distributed sensing and future logistics.

The vehicles will test autonomous navigation and cross-spacecraft communications while gathering information about the lunar radiation environment. NASA also plans cislunar communications demonstrations intended to reduce dependence on continuous ground contact.

An optical-imaging payload from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory will add another sensing objective. The mission will also reuse navigation software developed for the first CAPSTONE spacecraft, carrying operational experience into a more complex two-vehicle architecture.

CAPSTONE 02 is not a crewed mission and does not itself deliver a lunar base. Its value is architectural: prove that small spacecraft can coordinate, locate one another and exchange data in an environment where delays and limited ground coverage make autonomy useful.

NASA said human-spaceflight programs are funding the mission with support from the agency’s technology directorate. That pairing connects a relatively small demonstration to larger Moon-to-Mars planning without claiming the test is the only path to those goals.

Success will be judged after flight, not at contract announcement. For now, CAPSTONE 02 defines a practical 2027 test: two matched spacecraft, one lunar operating environment and a set of navigation and communications tasks designed to make future missions less dependent on Earth.

articles.body:
NASA astronaut Chris Williams returned to Earth after 241 days in space, landing in Kazakhstan with Roscosmos cosmonauts Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev after a mission that combined laboratory work with two spacewalks.

Soyuz MS-28 touched down under parachute southeast of Zhezkazgan at 5:27 a.m. Central time on July 26. The spacecraft had departed the International Space Station at 2:03 a.m.

NASA counted 3,856 Earth orbits and more than 102 million miles traveled since the crew launched on November 27, 2025. Those are mission totals, not distance along a straight line between Earth and the station.

The flight was Williams’ and Mikaev’s first. Kud-Sverchkov completed his second mission.

Inside the station, Williams supported research related to cancer treatments and in-space production of materials used in high-performance computers and electronics. NASA describes the work as research progress, not a completed therapy or commercial production line.

Outside the station, Williams completed two spacewalks. The work prepared power-system upgrades and replaced a faulty joint on the Canadarm2 robotic arm.

The landing closed an eight-month assignment but not the crew’s work. Post-landing medical checks and rehabilitation measure how long-duration microgravity affects balance, strength and other systems as the astronauts readapt to Earth gravity.

The mission also adds operational data for future long-duration flights. NASA uses the station to test research, maintenance and human-performance procedures relevant to later Moon and Mars missions.

The compact mission summary—241 days, 3,856 orbits and two spacewalks—captures scale. The substantive record is the combination of science, power-system preparation and robotic-arm repair accomplished during one first flight.Williams returned to NASA’s Johnson Space Center after the Kazakhstan recovery. The agency’s immediate account confirms the crew’s safe return and mission totals; detailed scientific results will depend on later analysis by the individual research teams.

That distinction matters for biomedical reporting. An experiment related to cancer treatment can test cells, materials or processes in microgravity without demonstrating that a treatment is ready for patients. NASA’s release describes the research area, not a clinical result.

articles.body:
NASA has opened a 25,000-square-foot wind-tunnel facility in Virginia that can suspend free-flying models in a 20-foot-wide vertical column of air moving as fast as 117 miles per hour.

The Flight Dynamics Research Facility began operating July 31 at Langley Research Center in Hampton. NASA describes it as the agency’s first major new wind tunnel in more than 40 years and a replacement for two aging facilities that shaped decades of aircraft and spacecraft testing.

Its purpose is not simply to push air past a fixed wing. Researchers can mount models on test equipment or let them fly freely inside the chamber, then study stability, spins, control, parachutes and the behavior of vehicles descending through an atmosphere.

The vertical test chamber is 20 feet in diameter, giving air more room to flow around larger and more detailed models. NASA says that improves the quality of measurements and expands the class of free-flight experiments the tunnel can handle.

Its maximum airspeed is twice that of the facilities it replaces. At 117 mph, researchers can fly heavier scale models and simulate some full-scale vehicles at higher altitude, where thinner air changes the relationship among size, speed and aerodynamic force.

The speed figure is a facility limit, not a claim that every test will run at the maximum. Researchers need controlled, repeatable airflow, and many questions about slow-speed stability or parachute behavior require lower settings.

The airflow comes from four 750-horsepower motors. Each drives a 14-foot-diameter fan with eight carbon-fiber blades, for 32 blades across the wind system and 3,000 horsepower of installed motor rating.

NASA says the lightweight blades allow the system to change airspeed quickly and precisely during free-flight work. That responsiveness matters when a model moves through the chamber and researchers need to keep it inside a safe test envelope.

The tunnel can support aircraft-safety studies, experimental X-planes, drones and autonomous vehicles. Its spaceflight work is atmospheric: models of reentry capsules, parachutes and landing systems, along with possible aircraft for Mars or other worlds with atmospheres.

Those uses are capabilities, not completed results. NASA’s opening announcement does not identify a first research campaign or publish validation data from a specific vehicle.

The new facility combines and improves the roles of Langley’s 20-Foot Vertical Spin Tunnel and 12-Foot Low-Speed Tunnel. The spin tunnel opened in 1941 and became a specialized place to study how aircraft enter and recover from spins; the smaller low-speed tunnel supported free-flight and control research.

Bringing their work into one modern building is meant to reduce maintenance demands and give research teams digital systems and a flexible test space. It is the fourth building delivered through NASA’s long-term Langley partnership with the General Services Administration.

articles.body:
NASA’s latest Earth indicator puts global mean sea-level change at 102.4 millimeters above its 1993 reference, with stated uncertainty of plus or minus 4.0 millimeters.

The agency describes the long-term rise as about 3.6 inches since satellite measurements began in 1993. The metric integrates observations from multiple altimetry missions rather than a single coastal gauge.

NASA attributes about two-thirds of current global rise to melting land ice and roughly one-third to thermal expansion as ocean water warms. Both mechanisms add height, but only melting glaciers and ice sheets add new water to the ocean.

The record includes seasonal movement. Water cycles between ocean and land through rain and snow, creating short-term rises and falls around the underlying trend. A single point should therefore be read in the context of the full series.

Mission continuity is crucial. Jason-3, Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich and other U.S.-international missions extend a measurement record built across changing spacecraft and instruments.

Global mean sea level is not a local flood forecast. Relative sea level at a particular coast can differ because land is rising or sinking, currents redistribute water, and storms, tides and atmospheric pressure create temporary extremes.

The ±4.0-millimeter range is also part of the result, not an optional footnote. It reflects limits in combining observations into a global estimate and means the displayed decimal should not be treated as perfectly exact.

For coastal planning, the global indicator supplies a common baseline. Engineers and communities still need local elevation, subsidence, tide and storm-surge data to design defenses or decide where adaptation is most urgent.

The signal is nonetheless unambiguous at the scale NASA reports: satellites have measured a multidecade rise. The accountability question now is whether infrastructure and land-use decisions use both that global trend and the local conditions that determine actual risk.

NASA publishes the indicator and mission context openly, allowing future updates to be compared with the same documented measurement series.

articles.body:
NASA’s Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer may have captured the clearest evidence yet that empty space changes the way light travels inside an extreme magnetic field, a quantum-electrodynamics effect proposed in 1936.

The target was magnetar 1E 1547-5408, a city-sized remnant of a massive star with a magnetic field more than a trillion times stronger than the strongest permanent magnets built on Earth.

IXPE observed the object for more than 140 hours between March and April 2025. NASA’s NICER instrument and Australia’s Murriyang radio telescope joined the campaign, producing the first coordinated radio and X-ray polarization measurement of a magnetar.

The neutron star rotates about once every 2.1 seconds. Its radio and X-ray peaks do not line up, indicating that the main X-ray hot spot is offset from the magnetic axis.

Researchers reported X-ray polarization degrees of about 40% and 80% in two modeled emission cones. The total polarization was nearly three times greater than measurements from similar sources and could not be reproduced by standard surface-emission models alone.

Vacuum birefringence offers a possible explanation. In a sufficiently strong magnetic field, quantum theory predicts that the vacuum acts somewhat like a lens or prism, filtering light according to its direction and increasing the observed polarization.

The team’s simulations reproduced the combined radio and X-ray signatures only when that effect was included. The result was published in Nature and NASA called it strong support for the long-standing prediction.

The language remains conditional for a reason. A model that requires the effect is not identical to a laboratory-style direct detection, and the researchers want more IXPE observations of this source and other magnetars.

The finding is nonetheless distinctive: an object thousands of light-years away may provide a physics environment impossible to build on Earth, turning X-ray polarization into a test of how the vacuum itself behaves.

articles.body:
Four commercial lunar landers are moving through assembly and ground tests as NASA tries to turn a sequence of one-off Moon missions into a repeatable cargo network. The most important word in that sentence is “tries”: none of the milestones NASA detailed Tuesday is a completed delivery.

NASA’s Aug. 4 update says Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines and Voyager Technologies are working toward lander flights by 2028. The agency’s first phase, running through 2029, calls for more than 20 robotic landings, with successive missions testing systems and placing instruments before additional human operations near the lunar south pole.

The update supplies an unusually useful snapshot of what is actually built, what is being tested and what still has to happen. It also shows why a launch target should not be confused with a delivery: each vehicle still faces integration, environmental or propulsion work before it can leave Earth.

Blue Origin’s uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1, named Endurance, completed an environmental campaign in NASA Johnson’s Thermal Vacuum Chamber A. The chamber recreated vacuum and extreme temperatures so engineers could evaluate structural and thermal performance before launch.

NASA says the lander’s structure, propulsion elements and avionics are fully assembled. It has completed communications checkouts with the Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System and Deep Space Network. The next major test NASA identified is loading cryogenic propellants.

Endurance is intended to demonstrate precision landing, cryogenic propulsion and autonomous guidance, navigation and control. NASA has assigned two payloads: cameras to observe how the engine plume interacts with lunar soil and a laser retroreflector that orbiting spacecraft can use for precise position measurements.

Firefly’s Blue Ghost Mission 2 pairs a lander with the Elytra orbital spacecraft in a stack NASA says is 22 feet tall—nearly three times the height of the company’s first Blue Ghost vehicle. The mission is planned for the Moon’s far side and is slated to carry three NASA payloads. Far-side operations also require a communications architecture that does not depend on a direct line to Earth.

Intuitive Machines’ third Nova-C lander, named Trinity, is being assembled alongside Altus-1, the company’s first lunar data-relay satellite. NASA says long-duration thermal-vacuum work on descent sensors is complete; engine integration and hot-fire testing remain. The planned manifest includes three payloads on Altus-1 and, on the surface, five NASA payloads, six commercial payloads and one civil payload.

Voyager’s Griffin-1 is undergoing environmental testing at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. NASA says the vehicle recently completed mass-properties testing, data needed for guidance, navigation, control and flight-dynamics models. The lander is planned to carry Astrolab’s FLIP rover with five NASA payloads, then return to Pittsburgh for final assembly after the JPL campaign.

NASA is also working with Northrop Grumman on three surface technology demonstrations derived from power and avionics hardware developed for Gateway’s HALO module. The demonstrations are meant to test survival through long cold periods, shared surface power and supporting avionics.

Those details matter because landing is only the first engineering problem. A durable lunar logistics system has to move payloads, communicate around terrain and the far side, distribute power and keep hardware alive through darkness and temperature swings.

NASA’s schedule remains a planning framework. Launch licensing, integration, test results, launch-provider readiness and lunar conditions can all move individual missions. The concrete news in the Aug. 4 update is the hardware status: one large cargo lander has completed thermal-vacuum testing, another is stacked with an orbiter, a third is in assembly and a fourth is in environmental tests.
