articles.body:
A new U.S. Geological Survey inventory puts two very different numbers side by side: about 355.8 billion short tons of available coal resources beneath federal lands in the lower 48 states, but only a little more than 4.2 billion short tons of reported reserves controlled by current federal-land mines.

The distinction is the story. A resource estimate describes coal known or inferred to exist under stated geologic and land constraints. A reserve is the smaller portion demonstrated as recoverable under existing economic and operating conditions. Treating the larger number as ready-to-mine supply overstates what the report establishes.

USGS counted 34 coal mines operating on federal lands in 2024. They produced 261,690,308 short tons, equal to 51.06% of total U.S. coal production that year, and 23 of the mines used surface methods while 11 operated underground.

The geography is concentrated in the West. Thirty-one of the 34 mines and more than 98% of reported reserves were west of the Mississippi River. Wyoming alone had 14 federal-land coal mines, including 12 in the Powder River Basin.

For the conterminous United States, USGS compiled 355.771 billion short tons of available federal coal resources. The Powder River Basin was the largest listed area at 180.89 billion short tons, followed by the Williston Basin at 27.16 billion and the Kaiparowits Plateau at 28 billion.

Those basin figures depend on the thresholds and exclusions in earlier assessments. Table notes vary by area, including limits on seam thickness, depth of cover, existing leases and permitted mine areas. The sum is therefore an inventory assembled from studies with different definitions, not one uniform mine plan.

Alaska adds still larger uncertainty. USGS identified at least 140 billion short tons of available coal resources there and said total identified and undiscovered resources may be as high as 5.5 trillion short tons. The report also says much of Alaska has not been adequately assessed.

Interior compared the resource totals with current annual coal consumption to describe centuries of potential supply. That arithmetic is a scale comparison, not a forecast that the coal will be permitted, financed, mined or burned at a constant rate for centuries.

Market demand, mine economics, transportation, environmental review, land-use decisions and energy policy all determine how much of a geologic resource can become a reserve and then production. The new report does not convert those contingencies into an extraction schedule.

The clean reading is narrower and more useful: federal lands contain a very large geologic coal endowment, current mines remain responsible for roughly half of U.S. output, and the portion reported as reserves is far smaller than the headline resource estimate.

articles.body:
Two unusually low-flying research aircraft are set to trace a tight grid over eastern Kansas, gathering magnetic and radiometric measurements for a new map of the rocks beneath the region.

The U.S. Geological Survey said flights could begin as soon as late July. The fixed-wing planes will follow preplanned lines about 980 feet, or 300 meters, apart while maintaining a nominal terrain clearance of about 260 feet, or 80 meters.

An Air Tractor AT-504 and a Pilatus PC-6 will carry sensors in an elongated boom, or “stinger,” extending from the main cabin. USGS said the instruments are passive, emit nothing that poses a risk to people, animals or plants, and will not collect photography or video.

The contractor, New Resolution Geophysics Exploration USA, will fly during daylight. Pilots are specially trained and approved for low-level work and coordinate with the Federal Aviation Administration, according to the agency.

Operations will be based at Coffey County, Salina Regional and Newton City-County airports. The announced route covers a broad band of counties from the Kansas City region south toward the Oklahoma line and west toward Salina and Wichita.

The survey centers on the Nemaha Uplift, a buried ridge extending from southern Nebraska into central Oklahoma. The region includes coal and petroleum resources, rocks with critical-mineral potential and the Humboldt Fault Zone, an active fault system that parallels the uplift.

USGS and the Kansas Geological Survey say the measurements can sharpen geologic maps used to assess mineral resources, geologic hydrogen, groundwater, earthquake hazards, infrastructure conditions and land-use questions. The flight data alone will not establish that an economically recoverable deposit exists.

The work is part of the federal Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, which combines airborne geophysics with geochemistry, lidar, hyperspectral surveys and field mapping. USGS says the resulting datasets will be released publicly through ScienceBase.

Because the planes will fly much lower and in straighter, more repetitive patterns than typical traffic, they may be conspicuous from the ground. The agency says the schedule depends on weather, aircraft availability and other operational conditions.

The mapped boundary is provisional. USGS listed additional counties in Kansas, Missouri, Oklahoma and Arkansas that could be added, so the final footprint may be wider than the initial blue outline.

bodyBlocks.text: The contractor, New Resolution Geophysics Exploration USA, will fly during daylight. Pilots are specially trained and approved for low-level work and coordinate with the Federal Aviation Administration, according to the agency.

Operations will be based at Coffey County, Salina Regional and Newton City-County airports. The announced route covers a broad band of counties from the Kansas City region south toward the Oklahoma line and west toward Salina and Wichita.
The target is the Nemaha Uplift—and more than minerals

The survey centers on the Nemaha Uplift, a buried ridge extending from southern Nebraska into central Oklahoma. The region includes coal and petroleum resources, rocks with critical-mineral potential and the Humboldt Fault Zone, an active fault system that parallels the uplift.

USGS and the Kansas Geological Survey say the measurements can sharpen geologic maps used to assess mineral resources, geologic hydrogen, groundwater, earthquake hazards, infrastructure conditions and land-use questions. The flight data alone will not establish that an economically recoverable deposit exists.

bodyBlocks.credit: U.S. Geological Survey

bodyBlocks.text: The work is part of the federal Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, which combines airborne geophysics with geochemistry, lidar, hyperspectral surveys and field mapping. USGS says the resulting datasets will be released publicly through ScienceBase.
What residents should expect

Because the planes will fly much lower and in straighter, more repetitive patterns than typical traffic, they may be conspicuous from the ground. The agency says the schedule depends on weather, aircraft availability and other operational conditions.
The mapped boundary is provisional. USGS listed additional counties in Kansas, Missouri, Oklahoma and Arkansas that could be added, so the final footprint may be wider than the initial blue outline.
The July 28 USGS media alert supplies the aircraft, altitude, flight spacing, survey boundary, sensor and public-data details.

A high-pressure heat dome drove temperatures to all-time records at sites in Montana, Utah and Wyoming on July 12, according to NASA Earth Observatory’s analysis of observations and weather-model output.

NASA’s map represents air temperature two meters, or about 6.5 feet, above the ground at 2 p.m. Mountain Time. It combines satellite observations with a version of the Goddard Earth Observing System numerical model rather than placing a thermometer at every mapped point.

The darkest areas approached or exceeded 45 degrees Celsius, or 113 degrees Fahrenheit. The broad ridge of high pressure covered much of the West and kept hot air in place while suppressing cloud formation and precipitation.

At airports in Billings and Miles City, Montana, temperatures reached 111°F and 115°F. Sheridan, Wyoming, reached 109°F. Each station exceeded its previous all-time record by at least two degrees; Miles City broke its prior mark by four degrees.

Those records have long baselines. NASA says the Montana station records extend to the 1930s, while the Sheridan series begins in 1907.

Multiple Utah locations also set all-time records. Deseret reached 115°F, placing it among the hottest labeled sites in NASA’s map.

A heat dome forms when a persistent ridge of high pressure promotes sinking air. Compression warms that air, while reduced cloud cover lets more solar energy reach the surface. Dry ground can further limit the evaporative cooling that would otherwise moderate temperature.

The mapped values and station records answer different questions. The GEOS analysis shows the event’s regional structure; airport instruments establish precise local records. Neither alone attributes the event to long-term climate change, which would require a separate attribution study.

The event was part of a wider period of Northern Hemisphere heat. NASA noted concurrent heat waves in parts of Europe and Central and East Asia, but the Western U.S. records in this report are tied specifically to the July 12 ridge.

articles.body:
Congress held two Iran war-powers votes on July 23. The House passed a concurrent resolution 214-208. The Senate rejected a motion to discharge a separate joint resolution 47-49.

Neither event, standing alone, ordered the military to stop fighting.

Understanding why requires separating the Constitution, the 1973 War Powers Resolution and the different forms of congressional action.

The Constitution gives Congress powers to declare war, fund the armed forces and make rules governing them. It names the president commander in chief. Presidents and Congress have disputed the boundary between those powers throughout the country’s history.

Congress enacted the War Powers Resolution over President Richard Nixon’s veto in 1973. The statute was designed to require consultation and reporting and to create procedures for ending military action that lacks congressional authorization.

The law generally requires the president to report specified deployments within 48 hours. Section 5(b) then provides a 60-day termination framework, with a possible 30-day period for safe removal, unless Congress declares war, enacts a specific authorization, extends the deadline or is unable to meet because of an attack on the United States.

The House used Section 5(c), which says forces engaged in unauthorized hostilities shall be removed if Congress directs removal by concurrent resolution.

A concurrent resolution must pass both chambers but is not presented to the president. The Senate did not approve the House resolution Thursday.

The Senate vote concerned a different device. S.J. Res. 180 is a joint resolution. If both chambers passed it, it would go to the president. The president could sign it or veto it, and Congress could override a veto only with two-thirds support in both chambers.

The Senate did not reach final passage. It rejected a motion to discharge the joint resolution from committee, preventing that procedural route from moving the measure forward.

The concurrent-resolution mechanism in Section 5(c) also carries a constitutional complication. In 1983, the Supreme Court held in INS v. Chadha that Congress generally could not exercise legislative power through a resolution that bypassed the Constitution’s bicameralism and presentment requirements. Chadha did not decide a War Powers Resolution case, but it cast doubt on the enforceability of Section 5(c)’s original design.

Congress later created expedited procedures for joint resolutions and bills directing removal of forces. Those procedures preserve presidential presentment and the possibility of a veto.

The House vote nevertheless has practical significance. It shows that a majority of the chamber does not accept the hostilities as congressionally authorized. It can shape oversight, appropriations negotiations and the political cost of continuing operations.

The failed Senate motion also matters. It shows that opponents did not have enough votes to force the separate joint resolution out of committee through that procedure.

Congress retains stronger tools than a one-chamber vote. It can prohibit the use of appropriated funds for specified operations, enact a binding joint resolution, pass a limited authorization for use of military force, impose reporting conditions or refuse future funding.

Each option requires more agreement than the House demonstrated Thursday. A funding restriction or veto-proof measure would require durable majorities in both chambers.

The most accurate description of the current position is therefore narrow: the House approved a removal directive, the Senate blocked a procedural path for a separate joint resolution, and military operations did not automatically end.

articles.body:
Section 301 is one of the federal government’s main tools for responding to foreign trade practices that the United States considers unfair.

It is not a single tariff. It is an investigative and enforcement framework established by the Trade Act of 1974.

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative can initiate an investigation into a foreign government’s act, policy or practice. USTR then determines whether the conduct violates a trade agreement or is unjustifiable, unreasonable or discriminatory and burdens or restricts U.S. commerce.

If the statutory conditions are met, the trade representative can take responsive action. Tariffs are one option. Other responses can include restrictions on services, suspension of trade-agreement benefits or negotiation of an agreement intended to eliminate the disputed practice.

The process matters because it produces an administrative record. USTR identifies the practice, publishes notices, accepts comments, consults affected governments, conducts hearings where required, issues findings and publishes the final action.

That record does not make the decision politically neutral or legally unassailable. The executive branch still defines the challenged practice, evaluates the evidence, connects it to U.S. commerce and selects the remedy.

The new forced-labor action illustrates the law’s breadth. USTR investigated 60 economies for failing to impose and effectively enforce restrictions on imports produced with forced labor. It concluded that the failures were unreasonable and burdened or restricted U.S. commerce.

USTR then imposed duties generally set at 10% or 12.5%, with exemptions and special calculations for several trading partners.

The United States has long prohibited imports produced wholly or partly with forced labor. USTR’s theory is that weak foreign import controls allow forced-labor goods to circulate through global markets, distort competition and undermine firms that avoid such production.

The remedy is not limited to a shipment shown to contain forced-labor inputs. It applies broadly to covered imports from an economy based on the agency’s findings about that government’s laws and enforcement.

That design raises several questions.

How closely must the remedy fit the challenged practice? A broad tariff affects lawful goods as well as suspect supply chains.

How will USTR decide that a government has improved enough to qualify for lower rates or removal?

What evidence distinguishes effective enforcement from a prohibition that exists only on paper?

How do the new duties interact with ordinary tariffs, Section 232 measures, trade agreements and product exemptions?

Section 301 has supported major trade actions for decades, including extensive tariffs on Chinese goods. Its flexibility makes it powerful. The same flexibility makes the quality of the investigation and the precision of the final notice especially important.

Readers evaluating any Section 301 action should look for five things: the foreign practice USTR identifies; the evidence supporting the finding; the statutory category invoked; the remedy selected; and the process for modification or termination.

The tariff is charged to importers when covered goods enter the United States. It is not a bill sent to a foreign treasury. Who ultimately pays depends on contracts, market power, supply alternatives and pricing decisions throughout the distribution chain.

Section 301 gives the administration leverage. It does not eliminate the need to ask whether the leverage is lawful, proportionate and likely to produce the stated result.

articles.body:
The Smithsonian Institution is federal, public, private and independent at the same time.

That unusual structure is central to understanding the Trump administration’s effort to influence the National Museum of American History.

Congress created the Smithsonian in 1846 to administer the bequest of British scientist James Smithson for the increase and diffusion of knowledge. The institution describes itself as an independent federal trust instrumentality and a public-private partnership.

It is not a cabinet department and is not organized as a typical executive agency.

Its governing authority belongs to a 17-member Board of Regents.

The chief justice of the United States and the vice president serve as ex officio Regents. Six members come from Congress: three senators and three representatives. Nine citizen Regents are appointed through joint resolutions of Congress signed by the president after nomination through the board’s process.

The board appoints the Smithsonian secretary, establishes major policies, oversees strategy and budgets and evaluates leadership.

No single branch therefore controls the institution cleanly.

Congress created the Smithsonian, provides substantial appropriations and participates directly in governance.

The president signs the joint resolutions appointing citizen Regents, and the vice president sits on the board, but the president does not ordinarily appoint the Smithsonian secretary or manage museum exhibits as the head of a cabinet agency would.

The chief justice serves as chancellor, bringing the head of the judicial branch into the same governing arrangement.

Private money matters too. The Smithsonian receives gifts, grants, research contracts and earned revenue in addition to federal appropriations.

This hybrid design was intended to support a national public mission while preserving institutional independence. It also creates multiple leverage points.

Congress can legislate, investigate and use appropriations.

The Board of Regents governs the Smithsonian and appoints its secretary.

Executive agencies can affect contracts, implementation and surrounding federal property where they possess statutory authority.

Private donors and partners can influence which projects are financially possible, though they do not possess formal governing power.

Trump’s July 24 order reflects those limits. Rather than directly ordering the secretary to rewrite exhibits, it tells executive agencies to examine laws, regulations, contracts and funding. It also directs the National Park Service to place signs on NPS-maintained approaches to the museum.

That could produce competing messages side by side: Smithsonian exhibits under the institution’s authority and administration-approved warnings on adjacent federal property.

The order may also provoke disputes over whether agencies are applying funding or contract conditions lawfully and whether they are attempting to coerce an institution Congress designed to have independent governance.

The Smithsonian’s Board of Regents has defended the secretary’s authority and described the institution as nonpartisan. At the same time, it has directed leadership to set expectations for unbiased content and report on changes.

Both the administration and the board therefore claim to be protecting accuracy and nonpartisanship. They disagree about the substance of those terms and who has authority to enforce them.

The practical answer to who controls the Smithsonian is: several institutions do, in different ways.

The Regents govern it. Congress created and funds it. Executive agencies control some money, contracts and property. Courts can resolve legal disputes when a suitable case reaches them. Private supporters exert financial influence without final legal authority.

That divided structure is why the current confrontation will unfold through implementation, appropriations, governance and possibly litigation rather than through one presidential command.

articles.body:
The World Health Organization has updated its dementia risk-reduction guidance, saying up to 45% of risk can be attributed to modifiable factors across the life course.

That figure is a population estimate, not a promise that an individual can prevent dementia. More than 57 million people live with the condition worldwide, and nearly 10 million are newly diagnosed each year.

The guideline recommends familiar health behaviors—physical activity, stopping tobacco use, reducing alcohol consumption and eating a healthy diet—alongside cognitive stimulation and social engagement for adults with normal cognition or mild cognitive impairment.

It also emphasizes medical risk management. Treating hypertension, diabetes and high cholesterol can reduce risks that affect both cardiovascular and brain health. Hearing aids may be offered as part of a broader strategy.

A new recommendation addresses air pollution, extending the guidance beyond clinical care and personal habits. Exposure depends partly on housing, transportation and environmental policy, so not every risk can be managed by individual choice.

WHO explicitly rejects several shortcuts. In the absence of a diagnosed deficiency, it does not recommend vitamins B or E, omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids, or multivitamin and mineral supplements for reducing cognitive decline or dementia risk.

The organization estimates dementia’s annual global economic cost at $1.3 trillion, about half driven by unpaid care from families and friends. That burden gives prevention policy significance even when no intervention eliminates risk.

The updated edition expands the evidence base used in WHO’s 2019 guidance and adds environmental exposure and tailored multidomain interventions. It also identifies areas where evidence remains insufficient.

For readers, the practical lesson is modest rather than magical: risk can be shifted through sustained health, social and environmental measures, but cognitive symptoms still warrant professional evaluation and risk reduction does not equal a cure.

Because the guideline targets health systems as well as clinicians, implementation also depends on whether services and environmental policies make recommended options realistically available.

articles.body:
The World Health Organization has launched a seven-part policy package to reduce drowning, a preventable cause of nearly 300,000 deaths worldwide each year.

Called PROTECT, the package moves beyond a single intervention such as swimming lessons. It combines physical infrastructure, rescue and resuscitation, occupational safeguards, water-transport standards, swimming education, child-care systems and preparation for floods and other hazards.

More than 90% of drowning deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries, WHO said. Drowning also remains among the ten leading causes of death for children ages 5 to 14, placing the problem at the intersection of public health, transportation and child safety.

The infrastructure component covers safer interaction with water. The transport component addresses standards for travel by boat, while occupational rules focus on people whose work regularly exposes them to water.

Skills remain central. WHO includes bystander and professional rescue capacity, resuscitation and basic swimming and water-safety education. Child-care and safeguarding policies are treated as a distinct layer because supervision failures can turn ordinary household or community water into a hazard.

The final component is threat preparedness. Floods, storms and other hazards can expose entire communities at once, and WHO says climate change is increasing that risk. The framework therefore links emergency planning with routine prevention.

WHO launched the package in Ghana, where it estimates about 1,100 drowning deaths a year—roughly three each day—with children and young adults disproportionately affected. The location highlights the burden but does not make the guidance Ghana-only.

A technical package is not evidence that deaths have already fallen. Governments still must adapt its recommendations, fund services, enforce transport and workplace rules, and measure outcomes consistently.

PROTECT’s main contribution is organizational: it makes drowning a systems problem rather than an isolated accident. That creates a clearer accountability test—whether countries build coverage across all seven domains and whether mortality declines where implementation is sustained.

articles.body:
No health-related Sustainable Development Goal is fully on track, and the information needed to measure some of the largest gaps still arrives too slowly, the World Health Organization says in its 2026 global statistics review.

The report is not uniformly bleak. New HIV infections fell 40% between 2010 and 2024. The universal health coverage service index increased from 68 in 2015 to 71 in 2023.

Other indicators moved backward. Global malaria incidence rose 8.5% from 2015, and WHO warns that disruptions, financing pressure and widening inequality threaten gains made in maternal, child and infectious-disease health.

The data system is itself part of the problem. At the end of 2025, only 18% of countries had reported mortality data within one year, limiting the speed at which new patterns can be detected and compared.

WHO estimates that 61 million people died in 2023. Only about one-third of those deaths had a reported cause, leaving models to fill large gaps in what should be a basic public-health record.

Cause-of-death information directs more than statistics. It affects how governments prioritize prevention, clinical capacity, vaccination, road safety and chronic-disease programs. Delayed data can keep an emerging problem invisible until later.

The pandemic’s full impact also extends beyond confirmed certificates. WHO estimates 22.1 million excess deaths from 2020 through 2023—deaths above the number expected without the crisis, whether directly or indirectly associated with COVID-19.

Those estimates carry uncertainty because countries differ in registration completeness and reporting speed. A modeled global total is necessary when records are missing, but it should not be presented as though every death was individually documented.

The 2026 scorecard’s sharpest conclusion is that progress and measurement cannot be separated. HIV prevention shows that sustained improvement is possible; rising malaria and incomplete mortality records show why targets can drift out of reach without financing, services and timely civil-registration systems.

articles.body:
Nearly two-thirds of Americans born from 1980 through 1984 received at least one form of work-related training outside regular degree-granting schooling between ages 18 and 38, according to a Bureau of Labor Statistics summary published July 27.

The National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997 found that 65.4% of the cohort received some form of training during that period. Formal employer training was the most common listed category at 29.1%, followed by vocational, technical or trade training at 26.5%.

Other reported categories included school-based training at 14.1%, training at work provided by an outside organization at 11.7%, training outside work at 11.1%, government training at 7.5% and apprenticeships at 3.6%. BLS also placed 14.3% in an “other” training category.

Participation differed substantially by educational attainment. BLS reported that 44% of people who had not completed high school received some type of training by their 39th birthday, compared with 61% of high school graduates who had not attended college, 71% of people with some college or an associate degree and 66% of people with a bachelor’s degree or higher.

The type of training also varied with education. Employer training reached 35.7% among people with a bachelor’s degree or higher, compared with 10.5% among people who had not completed high school. Vocational, technical or trade training was more common among high school graduates with no college and people with some college or an associate degree, at 32.3% and 32.5%, respectively.

BLS defines the training measure as instruction outside regular schooling that offers an academic diploma or degree. The category can include vocational and trade programs, apprenticeships, employer programs, government programs and other instruction intended to improve job skills, prepare someone for a new job or make it easier to find work.

The results come from a longitudinal survey that follows the same people over time rather than drawing a new sample each year. About 9,000 participants, born from 1980 through 1984, were first interviewed in 1997 when they were ages 12 to 17. They were interviewed for the 21st time in 2023 and 2024, when they were ages 38 to 44.

That design lets researchers measure whether a person received training at any point across roughly two decades. It does not describe the share of all workers receiving training in a single year, and it does not by itself establish that training caused later changes in wages, employment or job stability.

The survey represents people in this birth cohort who were living in the United States when the study began in 1997. BLS says it does not represent immigrants born from 1980 through 1984 who moved to the United States after 1997.

BLS reissued the underlying news release on July 17 to correct date and age ranges in one table and remove an extra digit from another table’s title. The agency said those corrections did not change any data estimates.

The findings show that training outside degree programs was common but unevenly distributed. Employer-provided training rose sharply with educational attainment, while vocational and trade training was most prevalent among people with a high school education or some college.

The data are cumulative through age 38 and specific to one generation. They provide a long-run view of how often early-1980s-born Americans encountered job training, not a real-time measure of the current labor market or the availability and quality of training programs today.

articles.body:
World Athletics has ratified eight record performances set during the first five months of 2026, making seven senior marks and one under-20 mark official across track, field, combined events and road racing.

The road performances are the most immediately recognizable. Sabastian Sawe’s men’s marathon mark was ratified at 1:59:30, while Tigst Assefa’s women-only marathon record was ratified at 2:15:41. Both were set in London on April 26.

On the field, Mondo Duplantis’s 6.31-meter men’s pole vault from Uppsala on March 12 became official. Simon Ehammer’s 6,670-point men’s heptathlon from Torun on March 21 was also ratified.

The indoor track set includes Khaleb McRae’s 44.52 in the men’s short-track 400 meters and a U.S. quartet’s 7:10.29 in the men’s short-track 4-by-800-meter relay.

Devynne Charlton’s 7.65 in the women’s 60-meter hurdles joined the senior list. Yan Ziyi supplied the under-20 record with a 71.74-meter women’s javelin throw in Xiamen on May 23.

Ratification is more than a headline repeat. World Athletics reviews record applications and supporting evidence against technical rules, including measurement, timing, course or facility requirements and anti-doping procedures applicable to the event.

The categories remain distinct. A women-only marathon record is defined by race composition, while short-track marks are separated from outdoor track marks. The eight numbers therefore should not be treated as directly comparable measures of dominance.

The ratified dates also differ from the announcement date. The performances occurred from February through May; the July 23 release records the governing body’s official recognition after review.

Taken together, the list shows an unusually broad record cycle: sprinting, hurdles, relay, pole vault, combined events, two marathon categories and a junior throwing event all reached newly certified marks before the midpoint of the year.

The announcement closes the administrative loop on those performances but not the season’s competition. Athletes may improve the marks, and new performances must go through the same validation process before they replace an existing entry in the official record book.

articles.body:
World Athletics has restored the under-20 5,000-meter race walk as a world-record event, reopening an official record pathway for junior competitors after a vote by the sport’s governing Council.

The decision took effect immediately following the Council meeting held July 1 and 2. World Athletics set inaugural standards of 18 minutes, 50.00 seconds for men and 20 minutes, 30.00 seconds for women after reviewing all-time performances.

Those thresholds are separated by one minute, 40 seconds over the same 5,000-meter distance. They function as entry points for the record category: an eligible performance must meet or better the relevant standard and satisfy ratification requirements.

The Council action does not automatically place a name beside either record. World Athletics still must receive and validate a qualifying performance under its rules, including the event’s technical conditions and the controls that apply to world-record ratification.

Race walking is judged by two defining technical requirements. An athlete must maintain visible contact with the ground, and the advancing leg must remain straight from first contact until the body passes over it. Infractions can lead to warnings or disqualification.

The restored 5,000-meter category creates a track-based benchmark for under-20 athletes that is shorter than senior championship road distances. Because it is expressed in an exact time, it also gives national federations and meet organizers a clear target when planning record-eligible events.

World Athletics did not publish the full list of historical performances it evaluated in the Council release. That limits independent reconstruction of why the two thresholds were chosen, though the governing body explicitly said its standards followed a review of all-time marks.

Any eventual record will depend on more than the clock. Eligibility, certified timing, course or track conditions, officiating, doping control and formal ratification can all determine whether a performance enters the record book.

For junior race walkers, the immediate consequence is straightforward: the distance once again has a recognized global record category. The standards define the gate, but the first ratified athletes to clear it will supply the names and performances that make the restored records real.

articles.body:
World Athletics added a career and media education program around the 2026 World U20 Championships in Oregon, extending athlete development beyond competition at Hayward Field.

Athletes Connect runs from Aug. 3 through Aug. 10 at the University of Oregon, covering the days before and during the championships. Its core program consists of four workshop sessions across Aug. 3 and Aug. 4, plus a separate athlete zone in Bean Hall.

Two sessions titled Your Athlete Journey focus on balancing education with sport, building a support network and planning for life after competition. Christian Taylor, Ashton Eaton and Ato Boldon were named as speakers for that track.

Two more sessions, Your Image, Your Power, cover media work, social platforms and using public visibility responsibly. Commentator Rob Walker and a major social-media platform were listed for those discussions.

Valerie Adams, the two-time Olympic shot put champion who now chairs the World Athletics Athletes’ Commission, was named to present the workshops. Her own progression from youth and U20 titles to a long senior career matches the program’s intended bridge.

The Bean Hall athlete zone adds educational games, printed materials and spaces for photography and video. World Athletics says professional content creators can help athletes produce material and provide guidance on posting and messaging.

The concept builds on earlier zones in Lima and Tokyo. More than 1,500 visits were recorded at the 2024 World U20 Championships in Lima across subjects including health and science, safeguarding, social media, athlete representatives and competition rules.

That number measures visits, not unique athletes or long-term outcomes. It shows demand for the space but does not establish that a workshop produces better contracts, safer representation or a longer career.

The initiative is nevertheless a notable addition to a global age-group meet. Many competitors are encountering international media, agents and sponsorship interest for the first time; Oregon 26 is treating those off-track decisions as part of athlete preparation rather than leaving them entirely outside the championship.

articles.body:
The World Bank Group approved a $20 million grant for a Central Asia water-cooperation project intended to strengthen shared data, prepare cross-border infrastructure investments and train regional institutions through 2031.

The Central Asia Water Efficiency Cooperation Project will be implemented by the Executive Committee of the International Fund for Saving the Aral Sea in coordination with participating countries.

The World Bank expects around 40 million people to benefit directly or indirectly from better regional water management. That is a projection tied to regional improvements, not a count of people already receiving a new service.

The underlying problem crosses borders. Aging infrastructure, weak regional institutions and limited data sharing affect the Amu Darya and Syr Darya basins, while droughts, floods and other extreme weather add pressure.

The bank says glacier surface area in the region has declined 30% over 60 years. It also estimates that limited cooperation among national water systems costs more than $4.5 billion annually through inefficiency.

By 2031, the project aims to prepare as many as six transboundary water-infrastructure proposals involving two or more countries. The areas include irrigation modernization, conservation, storage and coordinated operation of shared resources.

The program will also digitize water accounting and modernize information systems in both major basins. Up to 100 staff members from regional water-management organizations are slated for training.

Planning is not construction. A prepared project still needs technical review, financing, agreements and implementation, and the World Bank release does not guarantee that all six proposals will proceed.

The most immediate test is institutional: whether countries can produce compatible data, use shared platforms and make operating decisions across basin boundaries.

If that coordination improves, the $20 million grant could unlock larger investments. If it does not, the headline beneficiary and savings estimates will remain projections rather than measured results.

Public reporting should therefore separate institutional outputs from regional outcomes. Training 100 staff and preparing six proposals can be verified directly; economic savings, water reliability and benefits to 40 million people require longer-term measurement across participating countries.

articles.body:
The World Bank Group's Board of Executive Directors has discussed a new six-year partnership framework for China that would place greater emphasis on knowledge sharing, selective financing and lessons intended to apply beyond the country itself.

The Country Partnership Framework covers fiscal years 2026 through 2031. The World Bank described it as a new phase in a relationship that began in 1980 and has gradually shifted as China's economy and development needs changed.

The framework identifies three priority areas: enabling productivity-led growth and better jobs; strengthening human capital and social protection as the population ages; and expanding resilient, sustainable infrastructure while protecting and restoring natural ecosystems.

Those themes track priorities in China's 15th Five-Year Plan, including stronger domestic demand, job creation, updated social protection and the country's stated goals of peaking carbon emissions before 2030 and reaching carbon neutrality by 2060.

The World Bank said lending from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development is phasing down. The relationship is expected to rely more heavily on policy knowledge, innovation, mutual learning and targeted financing rather than broad development lending.

One part of that shift is the sharing of China's experience in areas such as ecosystem restoration, water management and agricultural productivity when other World Bank Group countries request it. The bank said those efforts would be linked to its Knowledge Bank and the China-WBG Global Center for Ecological Systems and Transitions.

The board discussion establishes the framework for cooperation, but it does not by itself set the value or terms of every future project. Individual operations and financing decisions would still require their own review and approval processes.

The World Bank said China is increasingly both a user and provider of development knowledge, as well as a contributor and donor to the institution. That evolving role is central to the framework's focus on ideas and practices that could be useful in other emerging markets.

The practical effect of the framework will become clearer as specific projects, advisory work and knowledge-sharing programs are announced during the 2026–31 period.

articles.body:
The World Bank has approved $375.9 million for equipment intended to stabilize Pakistan’s transmission grid and move wind power that existing bottlenecks keep from reaching customers.

The financing, approved July 9, covers the first phase of a 10-year program called Boosting Energy Security through Transmission in Pakistan, or BEST-PAK. Its immediate engineering focus is voltage control at high-capacity substations rather than construction of a new wind farm.

World Bank estimates say the upgrades can unlock 640 megawatts of wind generation now being curtailed and enable the full use of 1,840 megawatts of wind capacity in southern Pakistan. Those are project objectives, not power already delivered by newly installed equipment.

Plans call for static synchronous compensators, known as STATCOMs, at three major 500-kilovolt substations. These power-electronics systems inject or absorb reactive power quickly, helping operators keep grid voltage within limits when supply and demand change.

Fixed reactors and capacitor banks are planned across 26 additional substations. Reactors can absorb reactive power when voltage is too high; capacitor banks can supply it when voltage is too low. Together, the devices address stability limits that can force operators to reduce generation even when turbines are available.

The project is also designed to make room for about 491 megawatts of planned private-sector renewable projects. Whether all of that capacity is built and connected depends on decisions beyond this World Bank financing.

Pakistan has committed to a 60% renewable share in its electricity mix by 2030 under its climate plan. The grid project can support that goal, but it does not by itself guarantee the target, determine future demand or resolve every financial problem in the power sector.

The physical specifications respond to two hazards that can disable substations: flooding and heat. New installations are to use elevated platforms where flood exposure demands it, and equipment must be rated to operate at temperatures up to 55 degrees Celsius, or 131 degrees Fahrenheit.

Those standards matter because transmission equipment loses performance and ages faster when temperatures exceed its design envelope. Elevation can protect critical gear from inundation, but it cannot eliminate every flood risk to access roads, communications or connected lines.

The World Bank estimates the project could avoid about 832,500 metric tons of carbon dioxide a year, or more than 20.8 million tons over 25 years. That is a modeled impact. It depends on the upgrades being completed, wind power displacing more carbon-intensive generation and the grid operating as assumed.

BEST-PAK is framed as more than an equipment purchase. The first phase also supports Pakistan’s plan to restructure the National Transmission & Dispatch Company into specialized successor organizations and strengthen governance and operating performance.

Institutional reform introduces its own execution risk. Dividing responsibilities can clarify accountability, but only if staffing, control-room authority, maintenance budgets, data and emergency procedures remain coordinated across the new entities.

The approval is therefore a financing milestone, not completion evidence. Procurement, installation, commissioning and measured reductions in curtailment will determine whether the project produces its advertised capacity and reliability gains.

The most useful public checks will be operational: which substations receive equipment, when each system enters service, how often wind is still curtailed and whether voltage and outage indicators improve. Until those data arrive, the World Bank figures are a detailed plan with explicit engineering targets.

articles.body:
The World Bank approved a $1.02 billion financing package tied to energy and water reforms in the Philippines, pairing a large policy loan with a performance grant and targets for renewable power, offshore wind and local water utilities.

The Second Energy Transition and Climate Resilience Development Policy Loan consists of a $1 billion loan from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and a $20 million performance-based grant from the Livable Planet Fund.

Unlike a construction loan assigned to one plant or pipeline, development-policy financing supports an agreed package of policy and institutional actions. The announced measures include operating the Renewable Energy Market, incorporating electric-vehicle charging into utility planning and launching the country’s first offshore-wind auction.

That auction targets 3.3 gigawatts of contracted offshore-wind capacity by 2030. The World Bank said the broader reforms are expected to mobilize about $7 billion in private investment, a forecast that depends on investors responding to the new market rules.

The energy target is specific: renewables would rise from 30% to 42% of installed generating capacity by 2027. Installed capacity is not the same as electricity actually generated, because output varies by technology, weather, fuel availability and plant use.

The operation also addresses local water services. More than 1,600 local government units are responsible for provision, according to the World Bank, but many lack financing or institutional capacity. The reforms support cost-recovery tariff frameworks, a unified financing structure and bulk-water pricing regulations.

By 2027, the program aims to expand the number of local water providers with sustainable business plans from 10 to 100. The financing structure is designed to prioritize poor and climate-vulnerable communities, but the announcement does not list every provider that will qualify.

The policy loan builds on an earlier operation that established a legal framework for offshore wind, launched a reserve market, expanded retail-energy competition and created institutional groundwork for more sustainable local water service.

The numbers should be read as different categories: $1.02 billion is the approved public financing package; roughly $7 billion is expected private mobilization; 42% is a 2027 installed-capacity target; and 3.3 gigawatts is the offshore-wind auction goal for 2030. Delivery will depend on implementation beyond the approval itself.

articles.body:
The World Bank has approved a $1.5 billion development-policy loan for South Africa aimed at electricity, freight transport, ports, water and sanitation reforms rather than one standalone construction project.

The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development operation is the fourth in a series of standalone policy loans to South Africa since 2022. It is the first in that sequence to extend support into water and sanitation.

In electricity, the program backs a competitive wholesale market and more private investment in transmission. A concrete service target calls for 300,000 new household electricity connections by December 2027.

The announcement says load shedding has been virtually eliminated for a year and a half and private renewable-energy investment has increased sixfold. Those claims describe progress preceding the new loan and do not prove that every reform target has already been achieved.

Freight measures support competition among private rail operators and the country’s first port-terminal concession in Durban. The World Bank says rail and port freight volumes have risen by more than 50% since 2023.

Water reforms strengthen regulatory oversight, allow private service providers and give the new National Water Resources Infrastructure Agency more autonomy to invest in bulk-water systems. The World Bank expects household benefits even though it does not model large direct job creation from that sector.

Most of the employment effect comes from electricity and transport in the bank’s economic model: the equivalent of about 280,000 jobs by 2027 and more than 560,000 by 2032. The broader headline of nearly 600,000 includes modeled ripple effects and is not a guarantee.

Development-policy lending releases financing against agreed institutional and policy actions. It differs from a project loan with a fixed list of tracks, substations or pipes, making public reporting on implementation and outcomes especially important.

The measurable checkpoints are therefore the connection target, market and concession changes, infrastructure performance and household service improvements. The $1.5 billion approval is real now; the employment and service gains remain projections that South Africa and the World Bank will need to verify over time.

articles.body:
More than 1,700 young athletes from more than 135 countries are due at Hayward Field this week for the World Athletics U20 Championships, a five-day meet that opens Wednesday with three distance finals, the men’s shot put and a mixed 4-by-400-meter relay.

The Aug. 5–9 championships are the 21st edition of the global under-20 meet and the second staged in Oregon. The last Oregon edition was held at the former Hayward Field in 2014; the rebuilt stadium later hosted the 2022 senior world championships.

World Athletics’ most recent event release gives the expected scale as more than 1,700 athletes from more than 135 countries. Those are organizer figures, not a final count of starters: accreditation, travel and late withdrawals can change the field before each event.

The first champion is scheduled to come from the men’s shot put at 7:50 p.m. local time Wednesday. The women’s and men’s 5,000-meter finals follow, and the mixed 4-by-400 closes the opening session at 8:50 p.m.

The women’s and men’s 100-meter finals anchor Thursday evening. Friday concentrates on qualifying and combined-events competition. World Athletics lists 12 finals for Saturday evening and 15 titles on Sunday, when the championships end with the women’s and men’s 4-by-400 relays.

One new feature is the mixed 4-by-100-meter relay. World Athletics’ published program places its first round Thursday morning and the final Saturday evening. The mixed 4-by-400 remains on the opening-night schedule.

The U20 championships sit at an unusual point in the sport. The competition awards world titles, but the field spans athletes whose bodies, coaching environments and experience are still changing quickly. A standout performance can signal elite potential without guaranteeing a senior career.

That makes restraint important in covering the meet. Boho News will report verified results and competition records without turning teenage athletes into permanent projections or publishing unnecessary personal details. Athlete eligibility and official result lists remain the governing sources.

The event’s medals use the same geometric tree-and-wings form as the Oregon 26 logo. Organizers describe the tree as a reference to the state’s landscape and the wings as a link to the winged-foot symbol of track and field and Oregon’s “She flies with her own wings” motto.

Ribbon colors distinguish the medals: blue for gold, red and orange for silver, and green for bronze. Podium athletes are also due to receive matching pins intended for a coach, family member, friend or teammate.

Published schedules are operational documents, not guarantees. Heat assignments, advancement, weather and competition appeals can alter the order or timing. The official World Athletics timetable and results system should be checked immediately before any event or result is reported.

The reliable opening-day frame is broader: a five-day global junior championship returns to Eugene, introduces a mixed sprint relay to the U20 program and begins awarding titles immediately. The results from Hayward Field—not pre-meet projections—will determine which athletes leave with the new Oregon-shaped medals.

articles.body:
Global merchandise trade remained above its recent trend in the first half of 2026, but the World Trade Organization’s latest leading indicator shows momentum beginning to cool.

The WTO Goods Trade Barometer registered 101.7, down from 102.3 in January. Because 100 is the indicator’s trend baseline, the new reading points to above-trend trade volume with a weaker signal than at the start of the year.

The number is not a growth percentage. The barometer combines several forward-looking measures to show direction relative to recent trends; it does not mean world trade grew 1.7% or guarantee that the next quarterly volume report will match the signal.

Electronic components were the clear outlier at 105.5. The WTO connected that strength to demand associated with artificial-intelligence investment, which helped offset other pressure on trade during the first half of the year.

Transport measures still pointed to expansion. Container shipping stood at 102.4 and air freight at 102.2, although the WTO said both were expanding more slowly than a few months earlier. Export orders were only slightly above trend at 100.5.

Two goods-producing components were below the baseline: agricultural raw materials at 98.9 and automotive products at 99.8. The mix describes resilience rather than synchronized acceleration across every part of the trading system.

The WTO’s separate March outlook projected merchandise-trade growth of 1.9% in 2026 under its baseline and 1.4% in a high-energy-price scenario. It said sustained AI investment could add 0.5 percentage points, a scenario contribution rather than growth already booked.

The organization also noted that importers accelerated purchases before anticipated tariff increases in early 2025. That timing boosted year-over-year growth before it slowed later in the year, complicating comparisons with 2026.

The next trade forecast is scheduled for October. Until then, the barometer’s message is carefully bounded: world goods trade is holding above trend, electronics are doing unusual work in the index, and the aggregate signal is softer than it was in January.

articles.body:
The Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden will reopen its renovated outdoor space this fall with three new monumental heads by Yoshitomo Nara, beginning an annual series of artist commissions on the museum’s West Lawn.

“Yoshitomo Nara: Sentinels of Stillness” is scheduled to run from Oct. 31, 2026, through Nov. 7, 2027, the Smithsonian announced Tuesday. The presentation will bring “Long Tall Peace Sister,” “Smiling” and “Tiny Bright Round Eyes,” all dated 2025, to the National Mall.

Each work enlarges a palm-sized clay head Nara made in 2021. The finished sculptures are fabricated in aluminum and coated in white urethane paint, translating the irregularity of hand-shaped clay into forms intended for an outdoor public setting.

Hirshhorn Director Melissa Chiu said the show will establish a yearly West Lawn exhibition by a leading international artist. Anne Reeve, a Hirshhorn curator, organized the first installment, which the museum says will include free tours and art education.

The announcement describes the three heads as evoking childhood snowdrifts and as emphasizing how daylight changes across their surfaces. Those are the museum’s and artist’s interpretive frames; visitors will not be able to evaluate the installed works until the garden opens.

The new series is separate from the Hirshhorn’s permanent collection. The first show has a defined closing date in November 2027, and the museum says a different commissioned artist will follow on the lawn each year.

Nara’s sculpture practice predates the new works by decades. He began making figurative wood carvings in the mid-1980s, later worked with fiber-reinforced plastic, lacquer and urethane, and developed his ceramic practice during a 2007 residency in Shigaraki, Japan.

According to the Hirshhorn, Nara turned more deeply to hand-molded clay after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and Fukushima nuclear disaster affected his home region. He conceived large-scale sculptural enlargements in 2020 and made the small heads behind the new trio the following year.

The museum’s account is biographical, not a claim that the new works document the disaster. The announced sculptures are presented as contemporary public art shaped by material process, memory and scale.

The sculpture garden closed for renovation in 2023. Its redesign by Hiroshi Sugimoto received approvals from the Commission of Fine Arts and the National Capital Planning Commission in 2022 after public consultation.

The Smithsonian says the reopening will add an expanded entrance from the National Mall and refresh the passage connecting the garden with the museum building and plaza. Those access changes matter because the original 1974 sunken design could be difficult to enter and navigate.

The museum has not attached a separate ticket price to the exhibition. The Hirshhorn’s public programs and galleries are free, although operating details can change before the Oct. 31 opening.

For now, the firm facts are the artists, titles, dates, materials and planned series. The appearance of the completed installation, its relationship to the redesigned lawn and the visitor experience remain future-facing until the site reopens.

A decade-long international effort funded by the National Institutes of Health has assembled 665 patient-derived cancer models spanning 25 tumor types and tissue from 2,780 donors, creating a shared laboratory resource intended to speed precision-oncology research.

The Human Cancer Models Initiative, or HCMI, pairs laboratory-grown models with genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic and clinical information. NIH said the collection includes common cancer subtypes and many of the predominant genetic alterations within them.

Patient-derived models let researchers test questions that cannot be explored directly in a person’s tumor. The collection includes organoids that reproduce aspects of an organ’s cellular makeup and neurosphere clusters derived from brain cancers.

The central quality question is whether a model still resembles the tumor after it has been grown in a laboratory. HCMI researchers compared 421 tumors with their paired models and reported 97.8 percent agreement in genetic alterations, 95 percent concordance in epigenetic features and 92 percent similarity in RNA-expression patterns.

Those figures describe molecular agreement across the analyzed pairs; they do not mean every model predicts a patient’s treatment response with the same accuracy. A laboratory model is a research tool, not an individualized treatment recommendation.

The resource includes 522 models with detailed clinical data, 153 models of rare cancers and 71 models from people of non-European ancestry. NIH said models and associated data are being distributed through the American Type Culture Collection and an HCMI searchable catalog.

Researchers can use the models to study tumor evolution, drug sensitivity and treatment resistance. In glioblastoma models, the project identified several genetic features associated with resistance to temozolomide, a chemotherapy drug.

The work was published Aug. 5 in Nature with companion studies led by the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard and Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory. The compendium’s value will depend on how broadly researchers use it and how well later experiments reproduce clinically meaningful findings.

For now, the deliverable is concrete: a standardized, searchable collection that gives cancer laboratories access to hundreds of molecularly characterized models without each team having to build the same resource from scratch.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology will open two of its Gaithersburg research facilities for an evening public tour on Aug. 19, part of the agency’s 125th-anniversary program.

The event runs from 5:30 to 7 p.m. EDT at NIST’s Administration Building, 100 Bureau Drive. Registration closes Aug. 12, and NIST says the limited spaces will be allocated on a first-come, first-served basis.

Visitors must select one of two destinations when registering. The Million Pounds-Force Deadweight Machine calibrates sensors used to measure very large forces, including the thrust of aircraft engines and loads on structures.

The second option is the NanoFab at NIST’s Center for Nanoscale Science and Technology, where researchers use semiconductor-processing and characterization equipment to build and study technologies at very small scales.

The tour is limited to U.S. citizens and permanent residents because of site-entry requirements. NIST says the program is most appropriate for high-school age and older and that children under 12 will not be admitted.

Permanent residents must bring an unexpired green card. U.S. citizens using a state-issued identification card must present a REAL ID-compliant credential or another accepted federal photo ID, such as a passport or passport card. Digital copies and screenshots are not accepted.

The two facilities show opposite ends of the measurement scale: one creates precisely known forces approaching one million pounds, while the other supports fabrication and measurement at the nanoscale. Both are used to establish traceable measurements that other laboratories and industries can rely on.

NIST was founded in 1901 as the National Bureau of Standards. The anniversary program includes lectures, tours and partnerships throughout 2026; the Aug. 19 event is one stop in that broader schedule.

Registration is not a guarantee of entry if required identification is missing. Prospective visitors should use NIST’s official event page for the current capacity and access instructions before traveling.

Farah O’Keefe’s NCAA Division I individual championship has earned the University of Texas golfer an amateur exemption into the Standard Portland Classic, an LPGA Tour event scheduled for Aug. 13–16.

The NCAA and LPGA announced before the college championship that the 2026 individual winner would receive the place in Portland. O’Keefe secured it May 25 by finishing 12 under at Omni La Costa Resort & Spa in Carlsbad, California.

O’Keefe posted rounds of 69, 69, 68 and 70. She made six birdies in the final round, including birdies on the final two holes, and won by two strokes.

The title made O’Keefe the third NCAA individual champion in Texas women’s golf history, following Charlotta Sörenstam in 1993 and Heather Bowie in 1997. It was her fourth victory of the 2025–26 college season and fifth collegiate win overall.

The Portland exemption is part of a broader invitation that also covers the winners of the U.S. Women’s Amateur, Women’s Amateur Championship and Augusta National Women’s Amateur. The NCAA said 2026 would be the first year all four amateur champions were offered places in the same LPGA event.

An exemption gives a golfer entry into the field; it does not change amateur status by itself or guarantee a made cut. The event places O’Keefe alongside full-time professionals in a standard LPGA competition setting.

O’Keefe has already tested that level this year. Texas Athletics said she finished as low amateur at the Amundi Evian Championship in July, shooting 5 under and tying for 35th after four rounds.

Her college season included top-10 finishes in all 12 events, according to Texas, along with the ANNIKA Award and Honda Sport Award. Those honors describe past performance, while Portland will offer a separate test against an LPGA field.

For readers tracking the field, the useful distinction is simple: O’Keefe qualified through the NCAA champion pathway announced in March, not through a weekly sponsor invitation created after the fact.

The Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt reached its second-highest annual level in the satellite record in June 2026, while the Caribbean Sea and Gulf of Mexico each set regional records, according to NASA Earth Observatory and University of South Florida researchers.

NASA’s PACE satellite mapped dense concentrations across the tropical Atlantic. The western Caribbean held an estimated 3.6 million metric tons, the eastern Caribbean 9 million and the Gulf 5 million.

The Gulf total was nearly twice its previous record, which was set in 2025. Across the basin, 2026 trailed only the 2025 peak in the satellite record.

Sargassum is floating brown algae. In moderate amounts offshore, it provides habitat for fish, turtles, birds and invertebrates. Large nearshore mats can reduce oxygen, smother corals and seagrass and release hydrogen sulfide as they decompose on beaches.

The word belt can be misleading at local scale. NASA’s map shows a nearly continuous basin-wide feature, but it is made of discrete, moving mats whose paths depend on currents and winds.

Those patterns spared much of Florida’s west coast from heavy inundation earlier in the summer while steering more material toward the Florida Keys, the east coast and parts of the Caribbean, NASA reported.

PACE’s Ocean Color Instrument detects the algae because chlorophyll and plant structure reflect near-infrared light differently from seawater. Scientists use that reflectance signal to estimate the fraction of ocean surface covered in each pixel and then convert coverage to biomass.

The newer hyperspectral instrument builds on the longer MODIS and VIIRS record. Researchers said PACE observes more ocean and has greater sensitivity, which may improve winter mapping and help distinguish Sargassum from other floating algae.

June was the annual peak, not a statement that biomass continued rising afterward. NASA said newer observations showed a decline through July, and researchers are still investigating the mix of ocean warming, nutrient sources and biological feedbacks behind the belt’s longer-term growth.

The World Bank has approved a $100 million project for Argentina’s Salta Province that combines road rehabilitation, logistics upgrades, water and sanitation systems and new tools for managing growth in the mining sector.

The project will rehabilitate 24 kilometers of National Route 51 between Campo Quijano and Los Chorrillos. The bank said drainage and climate resilience are core parts of the road work.

Route 51 links high-altitude communities and production areas toward the Chilean border. The program also funds improvements at the General Güemes Logistics Hub and Industrial Park, which connects with the Belgrano Cargas freight rail network and the wider Bioceanic Corridor.

In Olacapato and San Antonio de los Cobres, financing is directed toward safe-water access and wastewater treatment. Those components make the operation broader than a transport loan.

The mining-governance track includes modernized information systems, digital platforms, environmental monitoring, technical training and transparency measures. The World Bank framed those systems as part of responsible critical-minerals development.

Approval establishes financing and project scope; it does not mean every road, pipe or digital system is already built. Procurement, construction schedules and performance measures will determine when residents see the intended services.

The operation is a variable-spread loan with a 32-year maturity and seven-year grace period. Those terms spread repayment over decades while leaving interest costs sensitive to the loan’s rate structure.

The combined design reflects a regional-development theory: road reliability, freight connections, basic services and public-sector capacity can reinforce one another. Whether they do so will depend on project execution and whether benefits reach the targeted towns and workers.

The most concrete near-term benchmarks are therefore physical and auditable: 24 kilometers of Route 51, named logistics facilities, specified water and wastewater investments and working public information and environmental-monitoring systems.

Singer-songwriter Amanda Pascali will perform a free concert at the Library of Congress on Thursday, Aug. 13, in a program celebrating the American Folklife Center’s 50th anniversary.

The concert begins at 7 p.m. in the Coolidge Auditorium. The Library lists Pascali as its 2026 Artist in Resonance and describes the program as a blend of folk and Americana with Mediterranean, Balkan and Latin influences.

Admission is free, but the Library directs visitors to register through its Live! at the Library ticketing system. The ticket also provides access to exhibitions and extended Thursday evening hours in the Thomas Jefferson Building.

Pascali’s concert is the middle of three highlighted August music nights. The month opened Aug. 6 with K-pop programs and an outdoor screening of Apollo 13, and it closes Aug. 27 with a Great Hall café concert by banjo player Tray Wellington and his band.

The American Folklife Center was established in 1976 to preserve and present traditional culture. Its archive contains songs, oral histories, photographs and field recordings gathered from communities in the United States and abroad.

The Artist in Resonance designation connects a working artist with those collections and with public programming. In this case, the anniversary concert foregrounds music shaped by migration and multiple regional traditions rather than treating folk music as a single fixed style.

Visitors during the Library’s Thursday evening program can also enter the Main Reading Room experience and current exhibitions, subject to the building’s access rules and capacity.

The event notice supplies the date, time, venue and registration path, but it does not publish a song-by-song set list. Attendees should not assume a specific repertoire beyond the musical traditions the Library identifies.

The Federal Trade Commission is mailing 9,419 refund checks totaling more than $672,000 to people who bought face masks and other personal protective equipment from Trend Deploy during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The agency says recipients should cash their checks within 90 days, using the deadline printed on the check. People with questions can contact the redress administrator, JND Legal Administration, at the number or website listed on the FTC's official refund page.

The distribution follows an earlier federal court order resolving the FTC's case against Trend Deploy operator Frank Romero. According to the agency, the business promised fast shipment of masks, including N95 products, and other protective equipment but did not consistently ship on time, offer required cancellation options or deliver the quality advertised.

Those statements describe the FTC's allegations and the basis for its redress program. The refund announcement itself does not calculate an equal payment for every buyer, and the agency advises recipients to use the amount on their individual check rather than dividing the headline total by the number of payments.

The most important fraud safeguard is simple: the FTC does not require a fee or bank-account information before a consumer can receive a refund. A message demanding payment, a wire transfer, gift cards or account credentials in exchange for an FTC check is not part of this distribution.

Consumers who receive a check should verify the administrator through FTC.gov rather than through a link in an unsolicited message. The official contact number for this distribution is 833-609-9714, according to the agency's refund page.

The case also illustrates the federal Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule. When a seller cannot ship within the promised time, the rule generally requires the seller to obtain consent to a delay or provide a prompt refund; the exact obligations depend on the transaction and the representations made.

The FTC says recipients do not need to submit a new claim for this mailing. Eligibility and payment amounts were determined from the redress records used by the agency and its administrator.

For affected buyers, the actionable details are the check, the 90-day cashing window and the official administrator. Anyone who did not receive a payment should not assume eligibility from the total alone and should use the FTC's published contact channel for case-specific questions.

OSHA's 2026 Safe + Sound Week begins Monday, Aug. 10, and runs through Sunday, Aug. 16, giving employers and workers a national prompt to examine how their safety and health programs operate in practice.

The Occupational Safety and Health Administration describes the week as open to organizations of every size and industry. Participation is voluntary, and the agency provides activity ideas rather than imposing a new rule or one-size-fits-all compliance checklist.

OSHA's recommended framework has three core elements: management leadership, worker participation, and a systematic process for finding and fixing hazards. The point is to make prevention part of routine operations instead of waiting for an incident to expose a problem.

Management leadership includes setting expectations, providing time and resources, and making supervisors accountable for the program. Worker participation means employees can report hazards, help design controls and raise concerns without retaliation.

The third element turns those commitments into a cycle: identify hazards, assess risk, select controls, verify that the controls work and revisit the process as equipment, staffing or tasks change.

A workplace can mark the week with a focused walkthrough, a short hazard-reporting exercise, a review of emergency contacts or a discussion led by workers who perform the task being examined. OSHA's materials encourage activities that fit the workplace rather than decorative events detached from actual hazards.

The calendar placement matters because a safety program is not proved by seven days of attention. A useful Safe + Sound Week activity should produce a documented action, such as assigning an owner to a hazard, setting a completion date or measuring whether a control reduced exposure.

Workers retain the right to raise safety concerns throughout the year. The awareness campaign does not replace employer obligations under the Occupational Safety and Health Act, applicable standards or state-plan requirements.

For organizations joining the event, the practical test is what remains after Aug. 16: a clearer reporting path, a hazard corrected, a worker included in a decision or a recurring review that did not exist before the week began.

The Smithsonian's ‘Voices and Votes: Exploring Democracy Across America’ remains on view through Monday, Sept. 7, in the Arts and Industries Building on the National Mall.

The exhibition examines the development of American democracy through sections on the system's origins, voting-rights struggles, campaigns and elections, civic participation and the responsibilities attached to citizenship.

Visitors encounter historical and contemporary photographs, video, multimedia interactives and objects such as campaign materials, voting memorabilia and protest items. The presentation treats democracy as an evolving practice rather than a finished institutional design.

This Washington installation is a special edition of a Smithsonian Museum on Main Street traveling exhibition that began circulating in March 2020. By the end of 2026, the Smithsonian expects the project to have reached 154 communities in 25 states.

That route is part of the exhibition's story. Small-town museums, libraries and cultural organizations developed companion programs about local history and civic engagement, and the Washington show incorporates some of those community voices through films and an interactive map.

The project is based on ‘American Democracy: A Great Leap of Faith,’ an exhibition developed by the National Museum of American History. Its subjects span the American Revolution, suffrage, civil rights and modern voting.

The Smithsonian opened the current presentation June 16 as part of programming around the nation's 250th anniversary. Private philanthropy supported the broader ‘Our Shared Future: 25’ initiative connected to the installation.

The exhibit's Sept. 7 closing date is the useful planning deadline. Individual programs and access conditions can change, so visitors should check the Smithsonian's official listing before traveling.

For readers outside Washington, the traveling network is equally significant: it shows how one national exhibition was adapted into local conversations rather than presented only at a central institution on the National Mall.
